Under 「詳細」, the 「断面の形」 「とがった」 makes pyramids of them, 「丸」 and 「半円」 cushions. 「Half-timbering」 and 「Stone wall」 are made for model buildings, such as the houses of a model railway or a diorama. 「Half-timbering」 raises beams out of the wall, the plaster between them lying lower: posts 「Panel width」 apart, a sill and a plate to every storey of 「Storey height」, and 「Rails per storey」 across it. 「Bracing」 chooses how much wood the panels hold: 「Braces」 lean towards the middle from both ends, 「St Andrew's crosses」 sit under the lowest rail, 「Corner braces」 in the top corners, and 「Mixed」 puts braces at the ends with crosses and corner braces between, as on many old houses. 「Beam width」 and 「Beam height」 make the beams wide and deep, 「Wood grain (%)」 gives them a grain: 0 % none, below 50 % more and finer lines, above it two wide, deep grooves – from planed wood to rough planks. As with bricks, panels and storeys are rounded a little so that whole ones fit, from the bottom edge up. 「Stone wall」 lays an old wall of stones of different sizes in rough courses, the mortar joints lower and every stone bulging a little by its own amount. 「Roundness (%)」 goes from broken stone with sharp edges (0 %) to rounded field stones (100 %); 「Size variation (%)」, 「目地の幅」 and 「ならび方」 say how different the stones are, how wide the joints and how they lie. Both are shape only, in one colour, so 「Pattern as its own part」 can make the beams or the stones a part of their own in a second colour. The pattern 「ひび（金つぎ）」 grows cracks across the surface as in kintsugi, with kinks, branches and a width that tapers towards the end. 「始まり」 tells where they begin: at the top rim of a vase or a cup, at the bottom, from the rim to the middle of a plate, or anywhere; under 「種類」 they become lightning. With 「金のうめものを別のパーツにする」 the notch is filled by a part of its own in gold, for a second filament; it goes along when you change or remove the texture. Under 「詳細」 you set branches, zigzag and chipped edges, and another 「シード」 throws the cracks anew. 「木の皮」 lays a tree's bark round a log: 「オーク」, 「マツ」, 「トウヒ」, 「シラカバ」 or 「ブナ」, each at its own size and depth. 「木目」 makes the body a piece of wood: under 「木」 choose oak, ash, beech, pine or walnut, under 「切り方」 a log without its bark or a board, flat-sawn with its arches or quarter-sawn with straight lines. 「年輪の幅」 makes the grain fine or coarse. With 「両はしに年輪を出す」 the ends of a log show the annual rings, and they match the grain on its sides: the rings run through the whole body as in a real piece of wood. Under 「詳細」 you add 「節」, and the rings bend round them. With the pattern 「文字（はりつけ）」 you stick a text onto the body like a label pressed on: the surface is unrolled round the place, so the letters keep their size on a vase's belly, on a slanted wall or over the edge of a box. "Around" (0° is the front, 90° the right) and "Height" in % along the axis say where it goes; with the axis on X or Y, 0° is the top - that puts the text on a flat plate. 「向き」 engraves it or raises it. Over a real corner it tears like a sticker; the status message says so then. 「文字を縦に並べる」 stacks the letters top to bottom here too. With faces picked, the text always lands on them, even where 「まわりの角度（°）」 and 「高さ（%）」 aim past them. To keep part of the body smooth, or to texture only a part, use a helper body: put a box, a cylinder or a sphere where it should be, select it and choose under 「テクスチャのマスク」 either 「テクスチャを付けない」 or 「ここだけテクスチャを付ける」. It turns transparent, and it counts when the other body gets its texture, also while it is hidden. Hide or delete it before printing. The result is a mesh like an imported model, and it keeps the body it was made on. Select it later, also after saving, and the card shows the settings it was made with: change them and click 「テクスチャを変える」, and the texture is made again on that body, where and as large as the textured body stands now. 「テクスチャを外す」 gives the plain body back. Mask bodies count again when the texture is changed: hide them rather than delete them if you may change it later. Undo takes back each of these steps as well. For a print in two colours, switch on 「Pattern as its own part」, with any pattern: the pattern becomes a part of its own, and 「Colour of the pattern」 gives it its colour – to begin with one that stands out against the body, the next time the one you chose last. Out of the body, the part is what stands out, and the body stays as it was; into the body, the body gets the pattern cut in and the part fills the cut up to the surface, like the gold of the cracks. Both go together in a bundle: they move together, each keeps its colour, and a 3MF has them as two parts for the slicer. Change or remove the texture as before; the pattern part goes along. With several layers, all have to go the same way, out of the body or into it; a pattern going both ways stays one with the body.

For a print in several colours, 「Paint」 colours parts of a body right in the design: a face, a round wall, the inside of a hole, a round patch or an area you draw round. It works like the paint tools of the slicers, but the paint is saved with the design. Select one body and click 「Paint」 in the 「変形」 group, next to 「表面テクスチャ」. The panel offers the colours of your design, and 「A colour of your own」 mixes one of your own. Then paint in the view with one of three tools: 「Fill」: a click fills the face up to its sharp edges, like the bucket of a paint program: the top of a box, the wall of a cylinder, the floor of a pocket or the inside of a hole, each in one click. 「Stop at edges sharper than」 says how sharp an edge has to be to stop the fill; at 90° it runs over the edges of a box. 「Circle」: a click lays a round patch of the 「Diameter」 set onto the surface, centred where you click, on a curved surface too. It stops at the body's sharp edges and never comes through on the back of a wall. 「Lasso」: hold the mouse button and draw round an area. What you see inside the shape is painted; the back of the body behind it is not. A box painted with the three tools: its top filled in yellow, a white circle on the front and a green star drawn round on the side, the Paint panel beside it. 「Eraser」 takes the paint off again with the same tools, 「Clear all」 takes all of it off at once. Every stroke is a step of its own, so Ctrl+Z takes the last one back. Between strokes the right mouse button turns the view as always; 「Done」 or Esc closes the panel. The edges of a circle or a lasso are cut into the body's mesh, so a circle on the face of a box is round, not a few triangles, and the body stays closed. The paint belongs to the body: it moves and turns with it, stretches with it when you resize it, and a stroke that finds nothing any more after a change is left out. A 3MF export writes the paint as painted faces, which OrcaSlicer, Bambu Studio and PrusaSlicer print with their filaments (see Files and saving); an OBJ keeps the colours too, an STL stays one colour. A group cut into one body, a box with its holes for instance, is painted as one body: paint it after cutting the holes, and its paint stays when you change the group in an open group. The parts of a bundle are painted one by one. A painted body that you group with others keeps its paint as a part and shows it again when you ungroup it. An imported mesh that is not closed is painted on its own triangles.

The 「花びん」 is a body of its own for vases, pots and lampshades. Its measures are under 「プロパティ」, its form and pattern on the card 「形と模様」; all of it can be changed at any time, also after saving: 「形」: bottle, bellied, bowl with neck, barrel, cylinder or funnel. The height and the widest diameter are the shape's own measures: drag the handles, or type 「直径」 and 「高さ」. 「断面」: a circle, a polygon with rounded corners or a wave (soft, pointed, arches or fins). 「ねじれ（°）」 turns it up the height, 「ゆれ（°）」 lets it swing back and forth. 「作り」: 「ソリッド（花びんモード）」 is for the slicer's vase mode (also called spiralize): the slicer prints one wall in a spiral and leaves out the top and the infill, so the body is drawn solid. 「壁のある中空」 gives a real wall and bottom for a normal print. With 「底」 at 0 mm the hollow vase has no bottom: a tube open at both ends, for bells, mouthpieces and pipes. 「模様」: a new vase is plain. To choose from are grooves, stripes, Voronoi cells or facets (low poly) on the outside, in a band of the height if you like; they belong to the vase and stay editable with it. 「上の断面」 blends the cross-section into a second one up the height, say from a circle at the bottom to a hexagon at the top. 「花びんを描く」, high up in the vase's settings, opens a large window of its own over the work area: in it you draw the vase yourself, in real millimetres. You move it by its title bar and make it larger from its corner; the vase in the view follows every change. 「形」 shows it from the side: drag the points, the top one sets the height, the widest one the diameter; 「ハンドル」 gives a point an angle, 「角」 a kink. 「断面」 shows the cross-section from above, and the 「対称」 mirrors or repeats what you draw. 「ねじれ」 draws the twist as a curve up the height. An SVG file from a drawing program becomes the cross-section or the body form, the mesh of a model vase (STL, 3MF, OBJ) the body form. A photo of a vase can go behind the drawing to trace, or 「輪郭を使う」 takes its outline. 「Trace」 does the same with settings: 「Threshold」 for how clearly the object must stand out from the background, 「Points」 (3 to 40) and 「Corner from」; the new body form shows in red over the photo first and becomes the vase's with 「Apply」. Where the vase stands before a busy background (a shelf, a room), the search does not find it; then the 「Magnetic lasso」 catches it: click roughly round the vase, between two clicks the line follows the edge by itself, and a click on the first point, a double click or Enter closes it. The body form then comes from the lasso; 「Discard lasso」 lets the search look again. One drag of the mouse is one step of undo; while you drag, the view shows the vase roughly. The card 「底と壁」 holds what the body needs besides its form. On a hollow vase: drain holes with a slope towards them, a hollow foot, an open wall (「すかしの壁」: Voronoi, honeycomb, diamonds or circles, for lanterns and baskets) and a 「ランプシェード」, hanging, standing on a socket or over an LED puck. On a solid vase, 「じょうぶな花びんモード」 cuts fine slits through which the slicer prints ribs inside or a double wall in its vase mode, in one go. Recesses for rubber feet go with either. 「水がもれないようにする」 raises the wall and bottom of a hollow vase to at least 1.6 mm. On the card 「付属品」 the vase gets its accessories. 「足」 can be moulded on, so they are part of the vase, or made to plug in, with sockets in the bottom; a stand holds the vase from below. A 「受け皿」 catches the water, or hides in the foot. A hollow vase can take an 「中に入れるもの」: a plant insert, one with a water store for a pot that waters itself, a holder for stems or water tubes. A 「ふた」 slips over the rim, snaps into a groove or screws onto a thread in the wall. As a 「Teapot lid」 the top of the vase itself becomes the lid, as on a teapot: 「Lid height」 (or 「Body up to · lid from」, from the bottom) sets how much, the pattern and the twist run on across the joint, a lip holds it in the opening, and 「Knob (printed apart)」 adds a knob that is glued into a hole on top. 「付属品をならべる」 lays the parts out beside the vase as objects of their own, ready to print, upside down where that prints better. The vase already has the sockets, groove or thread. After changing a setting, lay them out again: the parts from before are replaced. If a part does not fit this vase, the editor says so, for example when an insert would not get through a narrow neck. The card 「プリント」 tells what the vase takes to print: its weight in the chosen 「材料」 and the length of filament – for a solid vase worked out for the slicer's vase mode, one line along the wall. Below are notes on printing it: an overhang of more than 45° and where it is, a wall that is too thin, what a lid, a lamp or legs need, and the slicer settings for ribs and a double wall. A teapot lid is checked as it prints, upside down on its top: there a shoulder that narrows towards the rim overhangs. 「細かさ」 sets how finely the vase is divided into triangles: finer looks smoother, but makes the editor slower with large vases.
Selecting shapes, finding them in the object list, aligning, mirroring, rotating, laying flat on a face and multiplying in patterns.

A click on a shape selects it. With Shift you add more or take them away again. While Shift is held and two or more shapes are selected, a small number below the mouse pointer counts them. A click on empty space clears the selection, and so does Esc. Drag a frame on the empty workplane to select everything it touches; with Shift held, the frame adds what was not selected and takes away what was. If you would rather pick one part out of a cluster, switch on 「枠をドラッグする向きで決める」 in the settings (area 「外観」): a frame dragged to the right then takes only what lies completely inside it, one dragged to the left still everything it touches, and its line is dashed. Hold Alt while you drag to turn the frame around for that one drag, for example to take whole bodies from the side where the direction would not allow it. And Ctrl+A selects all visible bodies. While you drag a body or a handle of the frame, Esc cancels as long as the mouse button is still held: everything goes back as it was, and nothing is added to the history. A shape behind another one, such as a hole inside a body, you reach without turning the view: right-click the spot and choose 「ほかのものを選ぶ…」. The menu then lists every shape under the pointer, from front to back. The one your pointer is on is outlined in the view, even through the shapes in front of it; a click selects it, and with Shift it is added to the selection. The entry is there whenever more than one shape lies under the pointer; on a tablet, a long press opens the same menu. What is in your way you hide (「選択を非表示」, Ctrl+H). Hidden shapes stay in the design, they are just not visible and stay out of the export; the export window says beforehand how many there are. Ctrl+Shift+H brings them all back. What should stay put you lock with the padlock at the top of the settings or with Ctrl+L. A locked shape cannot be moved, resized, turned, recoloured or deleted: its handles turn grey, a padlock shows beside the arrow on top, and the tools that would change it are greyed out. Hovering a handle still shows its sizes, and a key that would change it says "Object locked". While one locked shape is in the selection, nothing changes for the others either. Hiding, renaming, copying and duplicating still work. To keep a part as it is and still build with it, lock only its shape: the shield beside the padlock, 「Lock shape」 in the right-click menu, or Ctrl+Shift+L. It can still be moved, turned, lifted, lined up, copied and grouped with others, but its size, its settings and its name stay as they are: the handles that change its size are gone, the fields for them are greyed out, and resizing, mirroring, ungrouping, the edge tools and deleting are refused. A copy keeps the lock, and so does the part inside a group, which can then be moved and taken apart again but not resized. The object list has the shield as well, beside the padlock: a part whose shape is locked always shows it, the others show it on the selected row and under the mouse, and a click on it locks or unlocks the shape. To work on a few parts deep inside a design, select them and choose 「Hide others」 in the right-click menu or under 「表示オプション」: everything else is hidden in one step, so Ctrl+Z or Ctrl+Shift+H brings it back. 「Invert selection」 in the right-click menu selects every visible shape that was not selected and lets go of the ones that were. Both are in the command search (Ctrl+K) as well, where you can also give them a key of your own. A number on the button of the group 「表示」 says how many shapes are hidden, and a click on it shows them all again. A design that is opened with hidden shapes says so once, with a button to show them. A part you hide while a group is open stays hidden when you close it with 「完了」: the group keeps its size and the parts left stay as they are, the hidden part still counts when the group is aligned, and showing all hidden shapes leaves it alone. Open the group again to show it.

With many parts it is easy to lose track in the view. The object list (「オブジェクトリストを表示」 or Ctrl+Shift+O) shows all shapes as a list. It stays open or closed as you left it, for every design, until you close it; the choice is kept in the browser. The object list: the group "Group" with two parts and a sphere beside it. A folder icon opens the group. A click on an entry selects the shape, including parts inside a group. With Shift held you add more entries or take them away again, just as in the view. The arrows fold groups open and shut. The label shows whether a part is 「ソリッド」 or 「穴」. Under the name stands what kind of shape it is. A body that is no longer a plain shape (rounded, hollowed or imported) says 「正確なボディ」 when the STEP export writes it exactly, and 「メッシュ」 when it is only triangles and goes as STL. A taper, lean or twist set after rounding or hollowing a body bends only its mesh, so it then says 「メッシュ」. Padlock and eye lock and hide single parts. 「名前を変更」 gives a part a name of its own; the pencil beside the name at the top of the settings does the same for the selected shape. Sensible names help enormously in larger designs. The A–Z button in the title bar (「名前を付けた図形をA–Z順に並べる」) sorts the shapes you have named alphabetically, with numbers counted as numbers (Part 2 before Part 10). Shapes that still carry their default name stay below in the order you added them, the newest last, and parts inside groups are sorted the same way. Only the list changes, never the design. A second click shows everything in the order added again, and the browser remembers the choice. The handle at the left of a row (six dots) moves a shape in the list: drag it up or down, or focus it and press ↑ or ↓. That changes the design's own order, the one the list returns to when the A–Z sort is off, and Undo takes it back. With the A–Z sort or a search on, the handles are hidden. To put a shape into a group, fold the group open with its arrow and drag the shape by its handle onto the group's parts; the group gets an orange frame. The shape stays where it is and keeps its name, and so does the group: a group is merged again with it, a bundle just takes it in. The parts of a folded-open group have a handle of their own: drag one out of the group and it lies loose again, at the place in the list where you drop it, or drop it on another folded-open group to move it there. A group left with one part is gone and leaves that part. Undo takes each of these back in one step. While you are editing a group, this is off. The search field finds shapes by name and by kind, so also "cylinder" or "hole". It also looks inside groups, however deeply nested: a group holding a match stays in the list and folds open to show the matching parts and the groups that lead to them. A group found by its own name shows all its parts when you open it. The arrow on the far left of the title bar folds the list down to its title bar and back. The list sits docked just right of the view cube. Drag it by its title bar to put it anywhere on the workplane; it passes underneath the view cube and the view bar. Drop it back beside the view cube, or double-click the title bar, and it docks again. Where it was and whether it was folded are remembered in this browser.

The card 「位置」 in the properties panel shows where the selected body stands, and you can type it: 「X」 and 「Y」 are the middle of its box on the plate, with the same signs as the distances shown on the workplane, and 「Z（高さ）」 is the height of its underside. With 「測るところ」 at the top of the card you switch to 「エッジ」: X and Y then show the body's left and front edges, so you put an edge exactly on a measure. The setting stays until you switch back to 「中心」. X counts to the right, Y towards the back and Z up, by the right-hand rule as in Tinkercad and CAD programs; the axis arrows on the plate show the directions. The values go in the unit you set, and the sliders reach as far as dragging does.

You can drag a shape past the edge of the plate and leave it there, about one plate width beyond each side, to keep it for later. The arrow keys move it as far as you like. A parked part still belongs to the design and goes into the export with everything else. To leave it out, hide it or export only the selection. If you have picked a printer, layerling warns at export when something sits outside its plate.

When you drag a shape across the workplane, it snaps to other shapes: its left, right, front or back edge or its centre lands exactly on an edge or centre of another shape. A pink guide line shows what it is holding on to. That way two parts sit flush side by side or centred one behind the other without typing numbers. It works with the grid switched off, too. The centre of the workplane counts too: the pink lines show when the shape sits in the middle of the plate along X, along Y or both. Hold Shift while dragging to keep the move on one axis: the shape follows whichever direction, X or Y, you have dragged further in, and leaves the other alone. Best press Shift once you are already dragging; on a shape that is not selected yet, a click with Shift only adds it to the selection. Or pull the red or the green arrow on top of the selection: it moves along X or along Y only, and the shape follows the mouse along that line even in a low view, where a free drag runs off far. The arrows snap as a drag does, Alt lets go, and afterwards you can click the distance moved and type the exact value. With Alt already held when the drag begins, you drag a copy, as in Tinkercad: the shape stays where it is and the copy lands where you let go. Pressing Alt only on the way pauses snapping; the shape then follows the grid only. A copy, too, snaps only once you let go of Alt on the way. To switch snapping off for good, use the grid menu in the bottom right (「シェイプにスナップ」) or the settings. For now only moving on the normal workplane snaps, not lifting and not resizing.

Two or more selected shapes are lined up with 「整列」 (L, or right-click the selection and choose it): points appear around the selection for left, centre and right, front, centre and back, and top, centre and bottom. A click on a point moves all shapes there. If you first click one of the selected shapes, it stays in place and the others line up with it. A locked shape in the selection is that fixed shape by itself. Left, right, front, back, top and bottom go by the box round a shape; the centre of a triangle, a pentagon or a star is its own middle, so a hole centred on one sits in the middle of the shape and not of its box. A shape turned at an angle, say by 45°, has its box round it to line up with, not its own edges. To line up with the edges, set a workplane on a face of that shape first (「作業平面を配置」, then click the face): the points then stand on the axes of that plane, and the shapes are measured and moved along them, as in Tinkercad. Reset the workplane to line up along the plate again. Align shows the possible targets as dots around the selection. The key is L. Esc cancels.

Hold Alt while aligning and the dots turn into squares: a click no longer moves the shapes but changes their size. A dot at a side stretches each shape to that side, its other side staying where it is, as if you had dragged its handle there. The dot in the middle leaves each shape in its place and gives it the width, length or height in that direction. That way you swap a box for a cylinder of the same size, say, or replace a broken piece of a mesh with a clean shape. Move over a dot with Alt held and you see beforehand how large the shapes become. The reference is the shape you clicked first; only the others change. Without one, the side dots stretch all shapes to the farthest side, and the middle dot gives them all the size of the largest. A cylinder stays round, so it grows in the other direction too. A shape turned at an angle stays as it is; shapes turned by 90° work.

Beside the middle point of each line stands a wider dot with a bar on each side. It spreads three or more shapes in that direction so that the space between neighbouring edges is the same everywhere, whatever size each shape is. The first and the last shape stay where they are, the ones between move. A row of holes of different sizes gets the same wall between them, for example. Move over the dot and you see beforehand where the shapes go; the status bar then tells you the gap. If a board (a base the others stand on, such as a flat box, not an SBC board) is among the selected shapes, longer in that direction than all the others, the shapes are spread on it: the gap at its edges is as large as the one between them, and a single shape comes to its middle. Shapes in several rows, such as the animals of a peg puzzle, are spread row by row; shapes whose boxes overlap across the direction form one row. Where the shapes stand in no clean columns, as the animals do from front to back, the shapes standing side by side move as a whole row instead. The whole puzzle then takes one click from left to right and one from front to back. Without a board, hold Shift and click an empty spot of the plate first: the plate is then the fixed shape, equal gaps spread the shapes over the whole plate with the same gap to its edges, and the other dots line them up on its edges or its middle. Another click with Shift on the empty plate lets it go. A click on empty space without Shift ends Align, as L and Esc do. Hold Alt and click the dot to type the gap yourself, say 5 mm: the shapes line up that far apart, starting at the first shape or at the one you clicked first; on a board the row comes to its middle. A locked shape stays where it is, so one between the outer shapes stops the equal gaps.

「ミラー」 (M, or right-click the selection and choose it) flips the selection across a plane: 「左右」, 「前後」 or 「上下」. Click the matching axis arrow. That is handy for symmetric parts: build one half, copy it and mirror the copy.

You rotate with the curved arrows on the shape, with the numbers in the settings or with R in 45° steps. When you drag on the rotation circle, the turn snaps to every tick, that is every 22.5°; hold Shift for finer steps, and extra ticks appear every 11.25°. Drag outside the circle to turn freely in 1° steps, or in 45° steps with Shift. Normally the selection turns about its centre. Sometimes it should not, for example when a tilted tube is to be turned further at its end. For that there is 「回転の中心を設定」: afterwards click on a face. A flat face supplies its centre, for example the axis of a tube end. On a group or a bundle the face runs on across parts that meet, as on one body, and the pivot goes to the middle of the whole face once the parts are joined, except on a group or bundle with text in it, or a bundle with a hole among its parts. The selection now turns about that point. A second click on the tool removes it again. The angles stay with the body. In its settings, 「回転」 shows them as 「X軸まわり」, 「Y軸まわり」 and 「Z軸まわり（高さ）」, named like the position: Y runs across the plate, Z is up. Type an angle there and the body turns to it - about its centre, or about its own pivot if it has one. While a turned body is selected, its angles also show below it on the workplane; 「回転したボディの角度を表示」 in the settings switches that off. A body turned about two axes: its angles stand under it, and the Rotation card in its settings takes them as numbers. With one body selected, the pivot belongs to that body: select other parts and come back, and it is still there. It moves, turns and scales with the body, is saved in the project and comes back with Undo. Under 「位置」 the pivot has its own X, Y and Z, which you can type or nudge, and 「削除」 takes it away. You can also drag the pivot's red marker with the mouse: it slides over the surface of the bodies and snaps to corners, edge midpoints and edges, so a hinge pin lands exactly on a corner. With several bodies selected the pivot is only for that selection, and a new selection removes it. Grouping or bundling them keeps it: the group takes the pivot as its own, with X, Y and Z under 「位置」. Hold Shift while dragging the red marker and it snaps to the centre of the face under the pointer instead - the axis of a round face, the middle of a flat one or the tip of a cone - looking through transparent bodies.

Should a part lie on its best side for printing? Select it, click 「面を下にして平らに置く」 and then the face that should go down. While you move the pointer over the part, the face under it lights up, so you see which one you are about to pick; turn the view to check the other sides. The part turns so that this face rests on the workplane. Two parts should meet face to face, or line up flush? Select the part that should move, click 「面を合わせる」, then click its face and after that the face of the other part. In the tool window, 「面と面を突き合わせ」 puts the faces against each other (back to back, touching), 「同じ平面」 lays them in one plane side by side; 「隙間」 leaves room between them, for example for clearance. 「合わせる」 moves the part: it turns the shortest way until the faces are parallel - not at all if they already are - and then slides only towards the other face, so it keeps its place sideways. The other part stays where it is, and one Undo takes it all back. The Align faces tool window: the part that moves is picked, a face of the other part comes next, then face to face or flush, and an optional gap. Holes on one axis: 「同軸」 lines up round faces instead: a hole over a hole, a pin in a hole, a screw in its clearance hole. Choose it before you click the faces. Then click the round inside of a hole (or the outside of a pin) on the part that moves, and a round face of the other part; the whole round face lights up while you point at it. 「合わせる」 turns the part the shortest way until the two axes are parallel and slides it straight across onto the other axis. Along the axis it stays where it was, so a pin keeps its height; push it in afterwards. This works on imported meshes too, as long as the hole is made of facets around one axis. A point onto a point: 「Point to point」 moves the part straight, without turning it, so that one of its points lands on a point of another part. Click a corner, a spot on an edge, the centre of a round edge or a reference point on the part that moves, then the point where it should land; a dot shows which point the pointer would take. Under 「Move along」 switch off the axes it should not move along: with only X and Y on, the point ends up straight above or below the other; with only Z on, at the same height. One Undo takes it back. Turning by a second and third pair: after 「合わせる」 the panel stays open for a second pair of points. The first point stays where it landed, marked in blue, and 「Turn」 turns the part about it until the line through its second point runs through the point you picked on the other part - so two edges come to lie on one line, even when the parts are not the same length. A third pair turns the part about the line through the two blue points until its third point faces the third point you picked, so the faces line up too - like aligning by three points in other CAD programs. 「Done」 ends it at any step; each step is one Undo. An exact angle between two faces: 「面を合わせる」 leaves the faces parallel; there is no tool of its own for an angle between them, but this gets you there. First bring the faces together with 「面を合わせる」, so they are parallel. Then set the pivot on the edge where they meet (「回転の中心を設定」, click the edge or a corner) and type the angle, 15 or 30 say, in the 「回転」 card of the part. It turns about that pivot. The card's axes are the axes of the plate, so this works when the edge runs along X, Y or Z. Just as simple are 「作業平面に落とす」 (D), which drops the selection onto the workplane, and 「作業平面の中央に置く」. With the workplane on a face, it centres on the point you picked with W and moves the selection only along that face, so what stands on it stays on it. Alt+D drops several parts as one piece: they all go down by the same distance and so keep their heights to each other, while D drops every part on its own. C picks the selection up, like Cruise in Tinkercad: it follows the mouse pointer and lies down on the face of another body you are over, sloped ones too. A click sets it down there, Esc leaves it where it was. Its underside then rests on the face, lined up with the face's edges as a new shape would be; it keeps its own turn about its up axis. Several parts travel together and keep their spacing. Over the empty plate, C stands a tilted part upright on the workplane again. Holding Shift while you carry sinks the part into the face instead: it stays upright, its top flush with the face and the body below it, which is how a countersink or a counterbore goes into a body; a new shape from the library is placed the same way with Shift held. Shift+D drops the selection with its top on the workplane instead of its base. Without a keyboard, the menu of a long press has 「面の上に置く」 for the same.

For hole grids, bolt circles and rings of teeth there is the 「パターン」. Select the shapes to be multiplied and click it in the ribbon. The pattern in "Circle" mode: the copies first appear as a preview. 「一列」: The selection is repeated at equal distances. The row steps along all three axes at once, with 「間隔 X」, 「間隔 Y」 and 「間隔 Z（高さ）」: one of them gives a straight row, two or three a diagonal row or a staircase. A negative spacing lays the row the other way. 「ボディ全体に並べる」: For holes along a plate, a key holder or a coat rack. Put the first piece on or into the body, choose 「Xに沿って」 or 「Yに沿って」 and set the 「端までの余白」: the original moves that far in from the nearer end (from the edge to the piece's side), and the last copy keeps the same gap to the far end. The spacing then follows the 「個数（元を含む）」: five holes or nine, they always fill the plate evenly. 「Grid」: For the holes of a perforated plate or a field of equal pieces. 「Columns along X (with original)」 and 「間隔 X」 lay the columns side by side, 「Rows along Y (with original)」 and 「間隔 Y」 the rows from front to back. One column or one row gives a single line. A grid has at most 100 pieces; past that the rows are cut back, and the window says so. 「円形」: The selection is spread around a centre. How many copies there are you set under 「個数（元を含む）」, and the 「全体の角度」 is 360° for a full circle. Choose whether the copies turn along. 「コピーごとの上昇」 lifts every copy a little more than the one before (a screw or an ascending spiral), and 「コピーごとの半径の変化」 moves it further from the centre or closer to it (a flat spiral); together they give a conical spiral. A spiral winds once around at most: an angle above 360° counts as a full circle, and there are at most 100 copies. Tip: first set the pivot on a face with 「回転の中心を設定」, then the centre of the circle lies exactly there. Afterwards the pieces keep the circle's centre as their pivot, also once grouped. That is where another part belongs, for example a ball in the middle of three legs: the middle of the pieces' box is not the centre, since three legs fill a box wider one way than the other. Right-click the pieces and choose 「回転の中心に印を付ける」, and the centre of the part you drag snaps onto it. The pattern in "Circle" mode with a rise and a radius change per copy: the copies climb and widen like a spiral. The copies first appear as a preview. Only 「作成」 creates them. If the copies are holes, group them afterwards with the body they should cut into. With 「コピーをグループにする」 ticked, 「作成」 groups the original and all copies into one object in the same step, as 「グループ化」 would: a ring of 36 pieces is then one part you can move, colour or cut with. Above 5 pieces the box ticks itself; once you tick or untick it yourself, it stays as you set it. 「グループ解除」 brings the pieces back. If grouping does not work out, the pattern still comes in as separate pieces and the message says why.

For vents, speaker grilles, baskets and enclosures the 「穴パターン」 spreads holes evenly over a flat face or round the wall of a cylinder. You no longer have to make one hole, repeat it and set it onto the wall. Select exactly one body and click 「穴パターン」 in the 「変形」 group of the ribbon, next to the pattern. You can also right-click the body, or find it with Ctrl+K. Click a flat face of the body. The whole flat face around your click counts, not just the triangle under the pointer. The round wall of a cylinder, a tube or a bore works too, see below; any other curved face does not: you get a hint and click a flat one instead. On a group or a bundle a face runs on across parts that meet, as on one body; on a bundle only when no hole is among them. The parts are joined shortly after the tool opens; until then only one part's face lights up under the pointer, and a click waits for the join. On a group or bundle with text in it, only one part's face lights up, and the click joins the parts. In the window, set how the holes look and lie: 「穴の形」: 「丸」, 「正方形」, 「長方形」, 「六角形」 or 「長穴」. Size: the 「直径（Ø）」 of a round hole, the 「一辺の長さ」 of a square one, 「幅」 and 「高さ」 for a rectangle and a slot. For the hexagon the size is the 「対角の直径（Ø）」. 「穴の角度」: rectangles and slots only: turns every hole in the face by that many degrees, counter-clockwise as you look at the face, from -90 to 90. The rows stay straight; if turned holes would come too close, even diagonally, layerling widens the spacing and the row spacing so a wall stays between them. 「壁を貫く傾き」: flat faces only, not with a counterbore, countersink or own shape: slopes every hole through the wall, from -60 to 60 degrees. On a standing wall a positive slope puts the inner end higher, so rain runs back out. The size stays the hole's own, so it shows a little longer on the face; both ends of each hole keep the margin. A slope only hides the inside when the wall thickness times sin(angle) is at least the hole's height, so use low slots or a thicker wall for that. 「Own shape」: repeats a shape from the scene in place of a hole: a rivet, a stud or the tread of a diamond plate. Choose it under 「Shape from the scene」. Its width and depth are the room it takes; it stands upright on the face as it was made, without its own turn. A body is set onto the face and joins it, a hole is cut in as deep as it is high. The shape itself stays where it is. 「Hole type」: round holes only. 「Plain」 is a straight hole, 「座ぐり」 adds a pocket for a cap screw's head, 「皿穴」 a 90° cone for a countersunk screw. The size is then the 「軸の直径」; 「頭部の直径」 and, for the counterbore, 「頭部の深さ」 set the head. 「ねじサイズ」 fills them all in for a metric screw. 「中心間の間隔」: the distance from one hole's middle to the next. If it is smaller than the holes allow, layerling raises it to the smallest possible value so a wall stays between the holes. For rectangles and slots it counts along the row, from left to right. 「列の中心から中心まで」: rectangles and slots only: the distance from one row to the next. So narrow, tall holes stand close side by side while the rows keep apart. A hole 2 mm wide and 14 mm high needs 4 mm along the row and 16 mm from row to row with a 2 mm wall. 「穴と穴の間の壁」: the same distance said another way: the wall left between two neighbouring holes, which is the wall thickness in the print. Set it and the spacing centre to centre follows (for rectangles and slots the row spacing too), and the other way round. For hexagons, rectangles and slots layerling measures the least distance between their edges. 「配置」: 「格子」 puts the holes in rows and columns. 「千鳥」 shifts every second row by half a spacing and moves the rows closer, so every hole has neighbours at the same distance - with hexagons that makes a honeycomb. 「Along the edge」: a ring of holes along the outer edge of the face instead, 「面のエッジからの余白」 in from it - screw holes round a lid or a plate. 「Spread by」 「Spacing」 keeps about the spacing, 「Number」 sets the 「Number of holes」; either way the spacing is evened out so the ring closes without a gap. 「A hole on every corner」 (on at first) puts a hole on each corner and shares every side out evenly between them. On a round face, or with the box unticked, the holes go evenly round from the top, and 「Start along the edge」 moves the whole ring along the edge. 「面のエッジからの余白」: the clear distance between the holes and the edge of the face. Only holes that lie wholly inside the face minus this margin are made; anything that would reach beyond it is left out. The margin also holds around openings in the face. 「深さ」: 「ボディ全体を貫通」 (the default) cuts through the whole wall. With 「カスタム深さ」 you give the depth in millimetres, for recesses, say. The holes show at once as a preview on the face and follow every value. The window says how many holes fit. 「別の面」 chooses another face, Esc closes the tool, and like the other tool windows it moves by its title bar. Only 「作成」 makes the holes. The holes are ordinary holes grouped with the body, just as after 「グループ化」: nothing is baked in. 「グループ解除」 dissolves the group again and frees every hole, which you can then move, change or delete one by one. The whole thing is one step for 「元に戻す」. The tool does not make more than 400 holes at once; make the holes bigger or the spacing wider then. The round wall of a cylinder, a tube or a bore takes holes too: a pen holder, a lamp shade, a tube with vents. Click the wall instead of a flat face; the whole wall lights up under the pointer. Every hole then points straight at the axis, and the rows go round the wall. On a wall that goes all the way round, each row holds a whole number of holes, evened out so the ring closes without a gap and never closer than the spacing; the window says how many go round and how far apart. The margin holds to the rims at the top and the bottom and to openings in the wall, on a part of a wall (a rounded edge, say) to its sides as well. 「壁を貫通」 cuts through the one wall you clicked and leaves the far side of a tube whole; on a solid cylinder the holes go in to its middle. Clicked inside a bore, the holes go outward through its wall. 「Along the edge」 is for flat faces and is not offered on a wall. An AI can do the same through the MCP bridge with layerling_perforate_face (see the chapter AI with MCP).

h: Pushing a face out or in
t: For a thicker wall, a raised pad on a face or a pocket cut into it, the 「面」 tool works on one flat face. It works on an imported STL too, where there is no sketch to change. Select exactly one body and click 「面」 in the 「変形」 group of the ribbon, next to the hole pattern. You can also right-click the body, or find it with Ctrl+K. Click a flat face of the body. As with the hole pattern, the whole flat face around your click counts; a curved face does not work here, a round wall neither. On a group or a bundle the face runs on across parts that meet, as with the hole pattern. In the window: 「向き」: choose 「外: 材料を足す」 for material standing on the face or 「内: ポケットを切る」 for a pocket cut into it. A pocket goes no deeper than the body behind the face; on a hollow body it can still reach the cavity. 「面のエッジからの余白」: how far the new outline stays inside the face's edge. Going out, 0 takes the whole face, which makes a wall thicker. Openings in the face grow by the same amount. 「角の半径」: rounds every corner of the outline, the inner ones too, so a sharp tip ends in an arc. A notch narrower than twice the radius closes, and a part of the face narrower than twice the inset and the radius together is left out. 「深さ」: how far the new part stands out of the face, or how deep the pocket goes. 「別のボディにする（グループにしない）」: with the switch on, the new part (or the hole of a pocket) is a body of its own beside the body instead of a group with it, so you can resize it, move it or use it to cut at once. The result shows at once as a preview and follows every value. 「別の面」 chooses another face, Esc closes the tool. Only 「作成」 makes it. What the tool adds is an ordinary sketch body, grouped with the body unless 「別のボディにする（グループにしない）」 is on (then 「グループを編集」 has nothing to open, and the part is free): nothing is baked in. 「グループを編集」 opens the group, and 「スケッチを編集」 on the new part shows the outline it follows. On the top or the bottom of a plain sketch body - one area, not grouped, mirrored, tapered, twisted or leaning, and without a stroke, key ring, fillet or chamfer - that is the body's own outline, set in when it is built, so its lines and arcs stay exact wherever the CAD kernel can set them in, for the edge tools and the STEP export. Resized later, the part keeps its inset. On any other face, and on every face of an imported mesh, the outline follows the face's triangles, and a curve is made of short straight pieces. The whole thing is one step for 「元に戻す」. To change the inset or the radius later, undo and run the tool again. To round the top edge afterwards, use 「フィレット」 with 「上端のエッジ」 on the group as the last step: like every edge treatment on a group, it joins the group into one body. An AI can do the same through the MCP bridge with layerling_push_face (see the chapter AI with MCP).

With several parts selected, the properties panel on the right shows how many there are and offers what applies to all of them together: 「ソリッド」 or 「穴」, one colour for all (a click on 「ソリッド」 opens the colours) and the lock. With a mixed selection, one click makes them all solids or all holes. If any of the parts is locked, only the lock can be used. Sizes are changed with the handles, with 「パーセントで拡大縮小」 or by typing a number into a size label. With several parts the number is the size of the whole selection: every part grows with it, the spaces between them too, as when you drag a handle. Solid and hole also work with a right-click or the S and H keys.

To make one or several parts larger or smaller by the same share, say all the parts of a print file by 20 %, use 「パーセントで拡大縮小」. Select the parts, right-click them and choose 「パーセントで拡大縮小」, or search for it with Ctrl+K. Under 「新しいサイズ」 you type the new size as a percentage of the current one: 120 % is a fifth larger, 50 % half the size. Width, depth and height change alike, so the proportions stay. The bottom stays where it is, so nothing sinks into the plate. With several parts you choose how they grow: 「まとめて」: The parts grow around their common centre, and the gaps grow with them. The whole becomes larger as if it were one part. 「各パーツをその場で」: Every part grows where it stands, and the gaps between them stay the same. The percentage field has the focus when the window opens, so from the keyboard it is Ctrl+K, the percentage, Enter; Esc closes the window. Only 「拡大縮小」 (or Enter in the field) changes the design, and one step back undoes it. With a locked part in the selection it does not open.

「元に戻す」 (Ctrl+Z) and 「やり直す」 (Ctrl+Shift+Z or Ctrl+Y) step through your history. How many steps travel with the saved design you set in the settings under 「履歴」. Point at either button and its tooltip names the step it would take back or bring again, with the measure where the step has one, such as "Rounded the edges of Box (5 mm)" or "Moved 3 objects (12 mm)"; the message after the step says the same. To go back several steps at once, use the history view below. A message that reports a step just taken, such as "3 shapes deleted", has an Undo button that takes exactly that step back.

「履歴」, next to undo and redo, opens a view of your history without changing anything. The work area shows the design as it was, and a slider at the bottom runs through every undo step: all the way to the right is the current state, each step to the left is one undo earlier, and states you have undone sit to the right of the current one. The arrow keys step through the states, Esc returns to the current state. The mouse wheel over the slider does the same, one state per notch, up to an earlier one; Page Up and Page Down jump ten states, Home goes to the oldest state and End back to the current one. You can turn and zoom the view meanwhile and click objects to bring them back (see below), but nothing can be moved; the design itself stays exactly as it is. If the bar covers something, drag it away by its title bar; a double-click on it brings it back. The list button in the title bar shows every step by name in a list, the newest at the top: a click on a step goes to that state, the state the design is at is marked 「現在」, and steps you have undone are grey. The list stays open the next time if you leave it open. The two play buttons under the slider run the history like a film: the one pointing right plays forwards from the state shown, the one pointing left plays backwards, each state for a moment, until the end; pressing the same button again pauses, and moving the slider, the wheel, the keys or the list takes over. Started at the end of its way, it begins again from the other end. 「Speed」 sets how long each state stays (slow, normal or fast) and is remembered for next time. Record the screen while it plays to show how a part came about. Two things you can take along from an earlier state. 「この状態から新しいプロジェクト」 puts that state into a new design in the overview, named after this one with the time of that state in brackets - a design saved before layerling recorded times says "copy" instead - and with the history up to that point, so undo keeps working there. 「この状態をエクスポートする」 opens the usual export with that state as the design, so you can save it as STL, 3MF, STEP, a picture or a LYL file with the history up to that state. You can also bring single objects back into the design. Click an object in the state shown - Shift+click adds more or takes one off again, a click on empty space picks nothing - and choose 「今のデザインに追加」. The view closes and a copy of each object lands in the current design exactly as it was in that state and at the spot it had there, selected, next to whatever the design holds now; nothing else changes. It is one step, so undo takes it back. Use it for a version of a part you changed since, or for one you deleted. A group comes back whole; notes and reference points on an object stay behind. Its name carries the time of that state, such as “Box (12:32)”, so it is easy to tell from the version the design has now. To bring back a part from inside a group, select the group and choose 「グループを開く」 or press E, as in the design: its parts are laid out where editing the group would put them, ready to pick, and the bar says which group you are in. 「外に出る」 closes it again. This is only to look - the group, the design and the history stay as they are. 「履歴を削除」 sits alone at the bottom left of the bar. After a question it removes every earlier step for good: the design keeps the state it has now (not the one shown), Undo has nothing to go back to and a file saved afterwards carries no history. Use it to share a design without its past, or to start the undo steps over. It cannot be undone; to share a file without touching your own design, choose 「なし」 when exporting instead.

How simple shapes become bores, slots and pockets, and how to change a group again later. This is the most important idea in layerling, and it is quickly learned: Every shape is either a solid or a hole. A solid stays. A hole is a tool that takes material away.

Select a shape and click 「ソリッド」 or 「穴」 in its settings. The keyboard is faster: H makes the selection a hole, S makes it a solid again. Both are also in the menu a right click on the body opens. A hole is shown see-through so you can see where it sits. T makes a body see-through, say to look into a housing; a second press makes it opaque again. It works on the whole selection: if any body is already see-through, all become opaque, otherwise all become see-through. As long as nothing is grouped, nothing happens with a hole. It just lies there and shows where something will disappear later. The cylinder is a hole. It sticks out of the top of the cube so that it cuts all the way through.

Select solids and hole(s) and click 「グループ化」 (Ctrl+G). Now the holes remove the material from the solids they touch. What remains is one single new shape. The result: a cube with a bore. This is how you get: Bores: a cylinder as a hole through a body. Slots: an elongated box as a hole at the edge. Pockets: a hole that does not go all the way through. Threads in a part: a tapped hole as a hole, see Threads and mechanics. If several solids are in the group, they are joined. Two solids that touch become a single part. With large meshes, such as an imported STL with hundreds of thousands of triangles, the cut takes a few seconds. layerling then works in the background and shows "「計算しています… そのまま作業を続けられます」"; meanwhile you can turn the view and use the interface. If you change the scene in that time, the result is dropped and layerling tells you so. The same goes for 「分割」. You can treat a group like a shape: move, rotate, colour, group again. 「グループ解除」 (Ctrl+Shift+G) dissolves it and the individual parts are back.

A whole group can also be a solid or a hole. A simple rule applies: If the group consists only of solids (or only of holes), you switch it as a whole and its parts go along. If it contains both, say a cube with a bore, each part keeps its own state. The whole group then becomes a tool, but the bore stays a bore.

h: Resizing a group: keeping holes and small parts
t: When a group is made longer, wider or taller, its parts stretch with it as if they were drawn on rubber: the round holes in a plate become ovals and move inwards. To keep them as they are, choose 「Keep holes and small parts」 under 「When resized」 in the group's settings; 「Stretch everything」 is what every group does until you change it. From then on, each time the group is resized - with the handles, the size fields or 「パーセントで拡大縮小」 - it is built again from its parts by one rule, along each direction on its own: A part that reaches across nearly the whole group, nine tenths of it or more, grows or shrinks with it and keeps its distance to both sides: the plate itself, a wall, or the inside of a box, whose walls stay as thick as they were. Every other part keeps its own size and its distance to the nearer side. A part in the middle stays in the middle. So a plate with a hole 5 mm in from each corner and a slot in the middle, made 40 mm longer, keeps its holes round and 5 mm from the corners, and the slot in the middle. There is no solver behind it and nothing to set up part by part: the same rule holds for every part, so you can tell beforehand what will happen. A turned part counts with the box it takes up in the group and stays turned; a group inside the group counts as one part. While you drag a handle, the group stretches as a whole; when you let go, it is built again, in the same undo step. Made smaller than a part needs with its distance, that part shrinks with the group as before, and a message says so. A mirrored, tapered or twisted group, and one with fillets, chamfers or a texture of its own, always stretches everything. Chosen for a group that is stretched already, the setting lays its parts out again at once. A plate with a hole 5 mm in from each corner and a slot in the middle, made 40 mm longer with Keep holes and small parts: the holes are still round and 5 mm from the corners, the slot is still in the middle.

Sometimes parts should only stay together without becoming one - a white logo on a black plate for a multicolour print, say. That is what 「バンドル」 (Ctrl+B) is for, as in Tinkercad. A bundle moves, turns and resizes like a shape, but nothing is merged: Every part keeps its colour and stays a solid or a hole. The bundle's settings have the same cards as a group's: 「ソリッド」 and 「穴」 for the whole bundle (which keep the parts' colours), 「透明」 (T) and 「マルチカラー」 (Shift+M); with Multicolor switched off the bundle shows and exports in one colour. 「パーツを分離」 takes the bundle apart, as Ctrl+Shift+G does. Holes cut nothing. When you group the bundle with other parts, its holes cut those parts but still not the bundle's own solids, as in Tinkercad. So a peg with its hole beside it, say, can be used again and again as a bundle. In an STL, 3MF or OBJ export every part is a body of its own; in 3MF and OBJ with its colour. 「グループ解除」 (Ctrl+Shift+G) takes a bundle apart again, E opens it for editing like a group. Chamfer, fillet and hollowing do not work on a bundle, because it is not one body: group it for that, or work on its parts one by one. If a hole in the bundle should cut the bundle's own solids too, take the bundle apart and group its parts (Ctrl+G).

「ブーリアン交差」 keeps only what two or more bodies have in common. Lay two overlapping shapes on top of each other, select both and click it. That turns a cylinder and a box into a piece with one round and one straight side. A group counts the way it looks, holes included. If a hole is selected too, what remains is what all the solids share with all the holes. If the shapes share nothing, nothing is changed and a message says so. The first click shows the common part before it is applied: the selected shapes turn see-through and what they share is drawn in green. Select and move each shape on its own and the green part follows; a second click on 「ブーリアン交差」 applies it, Esc closes the preview. Shapes with too many triangles for the preview, such as large imported meshes, are intersected on the first click. 「凸包」 wraps the selected shapes in one convex body, as if they were shrink-wrapped: the smallest body without dents that holds all of them. A half sphere on a cylinder becomes a dome with no step, four cylinders at the corners become a box with round corners, two spheres a capsule. Holes in the selection are cut out of the hull afterwards. The parts stay in it: 「グループを編集」 opens the hull like a group, and moving a part there and closing it builds the hull anew. The hull is a mesh, so round shapes show facets, and the edge tools work on it as on any mesh. When only holes are selected, the hull is a hole itself: two cylinder holes cut a slot. A hull fills whatever is hollow in its parts: a tube, a cylinder hollowed with 「中空にする」, a part grouped with its holes. Switch on 「パーツの穴を残す」 under Properties to keep them open: the hull then only fills the space between the parts, and a recess at the side of a part stays as well. 「クッキー型」 makes a cookie cutter from the selection: a thin wall round the outline, standing 15 mm high, and a flat rim of 2 mm round its foot, so the cutter stands on the rim and a thumb has something to press. Select one imported SVG or one sketch body and its own outline is used. A text lying flat gives its letters' own curves. Any other shape, a built one, an imported mesh or several parts, gives what it stands on: the outline the workplane cuts through it, so put it on the workplane first. Parts that overlap give one outline round all of them, as if they were grouped; parts apart from each other give a cutter each, in the same bundle. The outline is mirrored left to right: the cutter is printed standing on its rim and turned over to cut, so a text or a logo comes out the right way round on the dough. The wall's top runs in to a cutting edge 0.4 mm wide. Holes in the outline, the inside of an e or an a, get walls of their own, so they are cut out of the cookie too. They are a body of their own in the bundle, 「内側の壁」: to have a text or a pattern only pressed into the dough instead of cut out, make them lower under Properties. With a wall of 15 mm and dough 5 mm thick, inner walls of 12 mm press 2 mm deep. Inner walls lower than the outer wall have a flat top instead of the cutting edge: they only press, and an edge would leave thin tips that break off and grooves that hold dough. Give them an edge under Properties if you want one. Two bridges at the rim, on the side your hand presses, hold each inner wall to the wall round it, spread round it, 4 mm wide and 3 mm high. Each bridge stands with its whole width on the walls, in the middle of a side that runs along the outline, and never across another piece. Pieces side by side, such as the letters of a name, are also joined to each other, the closest first, so the bridges run as a web through all of them and a letter in the middle of a word is held as well. A click on the tool opens a small window: there you choose a 「板」 instead of the bridges, which fills the whole outline on the side you press, is steadier and sticks better to the print bed, but no longer lets you push the dough out from behind. 「フィレット」 puts small 45° slopes where the walls stand on the rim, the bridges or the plate, so thin parts such as the dot of an i do not break off; they are a body of their own in the bundle. There you also set how much lower the inner walls are and whether the outline is mirrored; the values stay for the next cutter. Change their height under Properties like the rim's. The cutter replaces the selection as a bundle of sketch bodies, 「グループを編集」 opens it. Wall, inner walls and rim are the sketch fill modes, a line outside the silhouette: change the thickness, height or colour of each under Properties, and the wall's 「刃」 there too (0 for a flat top). Where a tight bend leaves no room for a chamfer on both sides, the wall is bevelled on its outside only, to the same edge. Where an outline cannot be chamfered at all - a logo with sharp points, an outline cut from a body's triangles - the edge is built in fine steps of 0.1 mm instead, which a print layer of 0.2 mm cannot tell from the slope; such a wall is a triangle mesh rather than an exact body. To keep the outline as drawn, mirror the cutter back with 「ミラー」, 「左右」. A PNG or JPG picture works too: imported, it is traced into a sketch body, and the cutter follows that one. 「スケッチ間のロフト」 joins two sketch bodies or imported SVGs into one body: the outline of the lower one at the bottom, the outline of the upper one at the top, with straight walls between them. That makes a funnel, a transition piece from square to round, or a frame that narrows towards the top. Put the two bodies one above the other where they belong, shifted and turned if you like, select both and click the tool. The loft reaches from the bottom of the lower body to the top of the upper one. Each of the two needs exactly one outline. If it has a hole, a ring say, the other needs as many, and the holes are lofted too: two rings give a hollow wall. A sketch built as a line (a line outside, inside or centred under Properties) counts as such a ring. An imported SVG comes in filled; to make it a ring, give it a line under Properties. Both bodies must lie flat; the tool refuses tipped ones. The loft is an exact CAD body; the edge tools and the STEP export take it as one. The two sketches stay inside it: 「グループを編集」 opens them like a group, and moving or changing one there, or editing its sketch, and closing it builds the loft anew. 「グループ解除」 sets the two sketches free again. For two rectangles, circles or polygons there is also the Loft shape among the shapes, whose ends you set as numbers.

h: Cutting one body out of another
t: For parts that have to fit, a shaft in a collar, a bolt in a case, you make the one part and cut it out of the other. Select the two bodies and click 「型抜き」 in the 「結合」 area, or right-click and choose it there. The tool window names the part that stays and the body that gets the cavity; layerling takes the smaller one as the part, and a click on 「2つを入れかえる」 turns it around. The 「すき間」 makes the cavity that much larger than the part on every side: 0 fits exactly, 0.2 mm is a usual room for a printed fit. 「型抜き」 cuts a copy of the part out of the other body and leaves the part itself where it is. The result is a group: 「グループ解除」 takes the cut apart again. A clearance needs the part to be an exact body, like the 「オフセット」 tool, which it uses.

h: Punching an outline through a body
t: To cut the outline of one body straight through another, select the punch first and then the body to punch, and click 「打ち抜き」 in the 「結合」 area, or right-click and choose it there. The two need not touch: the punch can stand anywhere in front of the body, and only its outline seen along the 「方向」 counts, so a teapot held over a plate leaves a teapot-shaped opening. layerling starts with the axis along which the punch stands furthest from the body; X runs left to right, Y front to back, Z up. 「入れ替える」 turns the roles around, and the 「クリアランス」 makes the opening larger on every side, 0.2 mm for a printed part that has to pass through. 「打ち抜く」 groups the opening with the body as an exact sketch body set to hole, so 「グループ解除」 takes it out again; the punch stays where it is. Move or turn it and punch again for another opening.

If a bore turned out too small, you do not have to dissolve the group and rebuild. Select the group and click 「グループを編集」 in its settings, the folder icon in the object list, or press E. In the object list you can also open the group with its arrow and click one of its parts: the group opens with that part selected. A double click on the group does the same, as in Tinkercad, on a bundle too; if you would rather not, switch off 「ダブルクリックでグループまたはバンドルを開く」 in the settings. A part only starts to move once the pointer has been dragged a few pixels, so a shaky click or double click does not nudge it. The parts now lie separately and you change them with every tool: make a hole larger, move a body, add a hole. The group being edited: the bar at the bottom holds Cancel and Done, and the object list shows the parts. A bar appears at the bottom of the picture. 「完了」 rebuilds the group, with its name, its colour and its state as solid or hole. 「キャンセル」 puts it back untouched. If one of the parts is itself a group, you can edit it the same way, and so on as deep as your design goes. The bar shows where you are, for example "Bracket › Screw boss". 「完了」 and 「キャンセル」 always finish the innermost group and take you one level back out. While you are inside a group, only the groups among its parts can be edited; to edit another one, finish first. Unlike 「グループ解除」, which takes a group apart for good, editing keeps the group: its name and settings stay, and you can always go back with 「キャンセル」. A note: fillets and chamfers you had put on the whole group are lost on rebuild. The bar tells you so.

「分割」 in the 「変形」 area cuts the selection in two with a plane - a part too big for the print bed, say, or one you want to see the inside of. Select one or more solids or holes and click it. A translucent plane shows exactly where the cut will go, and a white line marks it on the bodies themselves, where the plane meets them; nothing changes until you apply it. 「平面の向き」: X makes an upright cut between left and right, Y between front and back, Z a horizontal cut between top and bottom. The axes are named as on the Position card, with Z up. The plane starts parallel to the workplane, so on the base plate with Z. 「作業面に合わせる」: 「平行」 lays the plane parallel to the workplane, 「Xを横切る」 and 「Yを横切る」 stand it square to it, across its X or Y direction. Where the workplane's origin crosses the selection the plane goes through it, otherwise through the middle. So you put the workplane on a sloped face with W and cut right there, without turning the sliders. 「平面の位置」: where the plane crosses, with the slider or typed in. It starts in the middle. You can also drag the arrow head on the plane; the plane moves along the arrow in 0.1 mm steps. 「面を選ぶ」, the button next to the position, lays the plane on a face: click it, then click the face. Orientation, both rotations and position are set to match. While you pick, a blue plane under the pointer shows the face it will take. A face of a body that is not selected works too, to line the cut up with it, but the plane stays within the selection. Esc stops picking and leaves the plane where it was. The two rotation sliders below turn the plane about the other two axes, up to 180° either way, for an angled cut. They can be combined. 「モデルを分割」 or Enter makes the cut, Esc cancels (while picking a face, the first Esc only stops picking). Every object the plane crosses becomes two closed bodies, named after their side, for example "Box (Z+)" and "Box (Z-)"; objects it misses stay as they are. A hole becomes two holes, and a hollowed body keeps its cavity. Both halves stay where they were - for printing, lay each one on its cut face with 「面を下にして平らに置く」. 「Connectors」 line the halves up again, as the cut tools of PrusaSlicer, OrcaSlicer and Bambu Studio do. With 「None」, the default, the split is as described above. 「Dowels」 makes a hole in each half and loose pins that go into both: the pins come as a third body, standing beside the halves on their floor, to print with them - standing, they come out round in the layers as their holes do, which is what the fit test measures. 「Plugs」 stands round pegs on the half whose name ends in a minus, with the holes for them in the other half. The connectors go in square to the plane, however it is turned, each with its diameter and 1.2 mm of material to every edge of the cut face, and two of them twice that apart. Each separate piece of the cut face gets its own, spread evenly over it: 「Per cut face (0 = automatic)」 says how many, and 0 leaves it to the piece's size, with at least two. A piece too small for one gets none, and a connector is left out where a half is thinner than its hole is deep; the panel says so before you split, and white rings on the plane show where they will go. If none fits at all, the parts are split without, and the status bar says so. 「Diameter」 is that of the pins and pegs, 5 mm to begin with. 「Depth into each half」 is how far each hole goes into its half. A dowel is twice that less 0.6 mm long and a peg 0.3 mm shorter than its hole, so they never stand on the floor of a hole and the halves close fully. Pins and pegs have a small chamfer at their ends, and each hole one at its mouth, so a first layer that spread does not narrow it. 「Dowels on a breakaway base」, with 「Dowels」, stands the loose pins on one plate that holds on to the bed, for a printer whose bed moves and makes standing pins wobble loose. Each pin rests on a small nub in a socket of the plate; once printed, bend each one to and fro to snap it off, as the fit test's pin can be. 「Clearance per side」 is the room between a pin or peg and its hole. Once you have measured your printer's play with the fit test (in the chapter on printing), it starts from that, otherwise from 0.2 mm. 「Dovetail」 holds the halves together without glue, like the dovetail cut of OrcaSlicer: a tongue that widens away from the cut face stands on the half whose name ends in a minus and runs straight across it, from edge to edge, and the other half gets the matching groove, open at both ends. Slide the halves together from the side, along the tongue; once in, they cannot be pulled apart across the cut. The tongues run the long way of the cut face, and where a body meets the plane in several pieces, they run the same way on all of them, so a half slides on in one move. 「Per cut face (0 = automatic)」 is the number of tongues side by side on each piece; 0 leaves it to the piece's width, one for every six tongue widths, at least one. Beside its wide top a tongue keeps half its own width and another 1.2 mm of material to the edge of the cut face, and two tongues twice that apart. A piece too narrow for one, or too short along it, gets none, and a tongue is left out where the other half is thinner than its groove is deep. White outlines on the plane show where they will go: the filled strip is the tongue's foot, the line about it its wide top. 「Width at the cut face」 is the tongue's width where it leaves the cut face, 6 mm to begin with. 「Depth into the other half」 is how far it stands out of the cut face into the other half, 4 mm to begin with. The groove is 0.3 mm deeper, so the halves close fully. 「Flank angle」 is how far each flank leans out from square to the cut face, from 5° to 30°, 15° to begin with. The larger it is, the wider the tongue's top and the firmer it holds. 「Direction (0 = lengthwise)」: 0 runs the tongues lengthwise, 90 across the cut face, and an angle between turns them that far. 「Clearance per side」 is the room on each side between the tongue and its groove, from your fit test as for the dowels. The tongue's ends are chamfered all round so it finds the groove, and the groove has a chamfer at its mouth. For printing, lay the half with the groove on its cut face, and print the half with the tongue the other way up, its cut face on top: the tongue's flanks then lean out by no more than their angle, which prints without supports. Holes are split without connectors. The halves are plain meshes: settings such as a cylinder's sides or a text's lettering are gone, so set those first. Ctrl+Z brings the original back in one step. Locked and hidden objects cannot be split. An imported mesh needs a closed surface to be split, grouped or cut. If it has openings, such as the eyes of a figure left open or a crack in a scan, layerling closes them with a flat cap first and says how many it closed. It closes small openings and flat ones of any size; a large opening whose rim bends is left to you, and the message says so. Close it in the program the model comes from, or with a mesh repair tool, and import it again.

If a shape consists of several separate pieces, such as text made of single letters, 「パーツを分離」 splits it into independent shapes. The entry is also in the menu you get with a right click on the shape. Tip: Always build holes a little longer than the part they are to pass through. If the hole ends exactly flush with the face, a wafer-thin skin sometimes remains. One millimetre of overshoot makes sure.
Chamfer and fillet on chosen edges, walls of equal thickness for boxes, cups and cases.

Sharp edges rarely look good on a printed part, and they are not particularly strong either. A chamfer cuts the edge off at an angle, a fillet rounds it. Both act on the edges you click. Select the body (or the group). Click 「フィレット」 or 「面取り」 in the ribbon, press B for the fillet or Shift+B for the chamfer, or right-click the body and pick it from the menu. The body's edges light up. Click those that should be affected. Another click takes an edge out again. With Shift you add or remove a single edge. Set the size and confirm with 「反映」 or Enter. Afterwards the window stays open on the new body with the same size, so the next fillet or chamfer can follow at once; 「完了」, Esc or the cross closes it. With Shift or Ctrl a click on 「上端のエッジ」, 「下端のエッジ」, 「垂直のエッジ」 or 「水平なエッジ」 adds those edges to the ones picked instead of replacing them. The "Fillet edges" tool: all sharp edges are selected, the picture shows the preview with a 4 mm radius. The tool window sits at the top right. If it covers edges you want to click, drag it away by its title bar; it opens there next time too, and so do 「中空にする」 and 「パターン」. Double-click the title bar to put it back. Picking a shape from the shape list while the tool window is open closes it without applying anything, and the edges you clicked are forgotten. The click then places the new shape instead of picking edges. In the tool window you find: 「すべての鋭いエッジ」 selects every edge at once, 「クリア」 empties the selection. 「半径」 for the fillet. For the chamfer you set 「距離」 or 「角度」. 「半径を変える」 (fillet only) lets the radius change along one edge: small at one end, larger at the other, evenly in between, as where a straight wall meets a slanted one. Click a single edge, then set 「始まりの半径」 and 「終わりの半径」. Which end counts as the start follows from how the edge was built; if the larger radius comes out at the wrong end, 「両はしを入れかえる」 turns it round. It works on one edge at a time, so round several edges one after the other. 「編集」 brings both values back. 「凹（えぐる）」 (fillet only) turns the fillet round: instead of rounding the edge off, it cuts a quarter-round scoop out of it, like the notched corners of a box. The scoop is a cylinder of the chosen 「半径」 lying along the edge, so it works for any angle between the faces, but on straight edges only, and not together with 「半径を変える」. 「編集」 brings it back. 「鋭いエッジのしきい値」 decides which edges count as sharp at all. A value of 25° treats only clear kinks as edges and leaves flat transitions alone. 「垂直のエッジ」 picks the edges that stand straight up, such as the corners of a box: one fillet then rounds all the vertical corners at once. 「上端のエッジ」 picks only the edges along the very top of the body. It is the quick way for a cookie cutter: build the outline in a sketch as a stroke, then chamfer the top edges. 「角度」 sets how steep the chamfer is; it cannot reach further than the wall is thick. 「下端のエッジ」 picks only the edges along the very bottom of the body, the mirror of 「上端のエッジ」. It is the quick way to round or chamfer only the foot of a part. 「面取りフィレット」, chosen at the top of the chamfer window next to 「面取り」, makes the printable foot of a part: a chamfer at the plate that blends tangentially into a fillet toward the wall, so the first layers need no support and the edge still ends soft. 「距離」 is the height the foot takes up, 「角度」 (15° to 75°) the steepness of the chamfer at the plate. Pick the edges with 「下端のエッジ」. 「見えているエッジのみ」 hides the edges that lie behind the body from where you look. By default every edge shows through the body, which gets confusing on a busy part; with the switch on you see, and can click, only the edges facing you. Turn the view to reach the others. An edge drawn in red (see below) always shows. 「クリックで、なめらかに続くエッジも一緒に選ぶ」: a click then also picks edges that flow smoothly into each other, for example all edges around a face with rounded corners. The switch only decides what a click picks: the CAD kernel always carries a chamfer or fillet on along such smoothly continuing edges. The tool window tells you along how many more edges that happens. 「サイズ変更時にエッジのサイズを保つ」 keeps the chamfer or fillet as large as it is, even if you scale the body later. 「プレビューの品質」 (「ドラフト」, 「標準」 or 「高品質」) decides how finely the preview is calculated. For difficult parts 「ドラフト」 is faster. The window keeps its settings in this browser, one set each for chamfer, fillet and chamfer-fillet: size, angle, threshold, preview quality and the switches stay as you left them after 「反映」, after an undo and the next time you open the tool. A size the body cannot take gives way to the one worked out from the body. Only 「クリックで、なめらかに続くエッジも一緒に選ぶ」 starts anew: on for a body's first chamfer or fillet, off after that. While you adjust the size, layerling recalculates the preview. It can take a moment. You may keep adjusting; the last value you chose is what gets calculated. If the size is too large for the edge, layerling says so and suggests a smaller value. Often one or two millimetres less will do. At sharp angles a fillet needs more room than its radius suggests. On a small screen the tool window scrolls down by itself so the message is in view. When a selection that worked fails after you click one more edge, that edge turns red and is drawn wider: it is the one that cannot be treated together with the others at this size. Click it again to take it out, or make the size smaller. If you click more edges while the message stands, the first one stays red. When there is no earlier selection that worked - the very first click, or a size you just raised - the edges that fail even on their own turn red, or all of them if it is only their combination. A fillet along a curved edge has one more limit. Where the edge bends round the outside of the body tighter than the radius, as at the tip of a drop drawn in a sketch or brought in as an SVG, the rounding cannot follow the bend. layerling then says how tight the tightest bend is and draws the edges that have it in red.
