Choose a radius smaller than that, or draw the bend rounder. A sharp corner is no such bend: two edges meet there, and each is rounded on its own. So round the top edges before you round a corner with a small radius: the rounded corner would be a tight bend for the top. Before it gives up, layerling tries once more with the short edges at the ends of the picked ones, up to twice the size long. One sits where an earlier chamfer ends on a wall that is still sharp: a short slanted edge in the corner, and the corner cannot be treated while it stays sharp. If that helps, those edges are picked as well, and a message says how many were taken along. And where the picked edges meet in a sharp inner corner, as two discs of a cloud do, a fillet has no room at any size: layerling then rounds those corners first, at the same size or a smaller one, and the message says how many and how much (a chamfer chamfers them). The edge under the pointer is drawn wider too, so you can see which one a click will pick. A hole takes 「面取り」 and 「フィレット」 as well, and so do 「中空にする」, 「オフセット」 and 「面を削除」: it stays a hole and cuts with its new shape. Rounding the four upright edges of a box hole cuts a pocket with round inside corners, and a hole grown with 「オフセット」 cuts with that much more room. To break the edge where a hole meets the part, treat the finished group instead: that edge belongs to it.

A treated body can always be treated again. Select it again and open the tool - Fillet, Chamfer or Hollow, each shows the list: under 「エッジ処理を元に戻す」 you see what is already on it. 「元に戻す」 takes back a single treatment. Note: if newer treatments lie on top, they go with it, and the tool window tells you how many. Next to a chamfer, a fillet or a hollowing there is also 「編集」. It takes the treatment back the same way, but opens the tool again at once with the same edges and the old value. You change the value and apply it again: a 3 mm fillet becomes a 5 mm one without clicking the edges once more. If newer treatments lie on top, they go with it here too. This holds for edge treatments you make from now on; older ones only offer taking back, and so do single parts of a group. On a group, say a cylinder with a hole, the treated edge belongs to the finished body, not to one of its parts. So the group becomes a single body. 「グループ解除」 still works on it: it takes the edge features back first and then dissolves the group, in one step that Ctrl+Z undoes. Take the treatment back as described above and the group returns with all its parts. The easiest way is to treat edges last. That goes for threads too: the edge tool takes a thread as its exact body, so a block with a tapped hole in it gets its edges rounded with the thread in place. Working out a thread's edges takes longer than for a plain shape, a few seconds for an M6 and about half a minute for a G1/2 pipe thread. Good to know: layerling works with real CAD geometry for fillets and chamfers, not just a triangle mesh. That is why a rounded edge is still a rounded edge in the STEP export. A part imported as STEP keeps its CAD geometry too: chamfers, fillets and hollowing work on the body from the file, however finely the part is drawn on screen. STL, OBJ and 3MF bring only triangles, and a finely drawn part can be too dense for the edge tool. If a part is also available as STEP, import that. 「Make exact」 turns such a part into an exact body with real planes and cylinders first, see Files, saving and sharing, "Making an imported mesh exact".

Boxes, cups, cases and covers have one thing in common: they are empty inside, with walls of equal thickness. That is exactly what 「中空にする」 does. Select the body and click 「中空にする」, or right-click the body and pick it from the menu. Set the 「壁の厚さ」. Under 「開ける側」, switch on the sides that stay open: 「上」, 「下」, 「前」, 「後ろ」, 「左」 or 「右」, as many as you like - 「前」 alone makes a slot for a drawer, 「左」 and 「右」 a tunnel. With no side switched on the body stays closed all round, with a cavity in the middle. 「閉じる (内部が空洞)」 switches every side off in one click. 「上」 is already on when the tool window opens; a click on it closes the top again. A body closed all round looks unchanged from outside: the section view shows the cavity. Decide whether the 「内側のエッジ」 should be 「丸める」 or 「鋭く」. Click 「中空にする」. The hollowing tool window with wall thickness, a switch for each side that stays open, and the inner edges. The walls grow inward. The outside stays as it is. The 「内側のエッジ」 only matter where the inner walls move apart - at a step in the body or around an opening. The corners of the cavity of a plain box are always sharp, with both settings. For a rounded inside, round the outside edges of the body first (see above), then hollow it: the inside follows with the radius minus the wall thickness. If the rounded inside cannot be built, which can happen with an outline made of very many short straight pieces such as a traced drawing, layerling builds the same hollow body with sharp inner corners instead. The result: a shell with a 3 mm wall, open at the top. The same box with only the front side open: a slot for a drawer. For every open side, the body needs a flat face at its very edge on that side. Spheres and free-form shapes therefore cannot be hollowed this way. If the wall is too thick for the body, layerling tells you and asks for a thinner one. A rounded box whose top and bottom edges are rounded as well is such a case: its wall has to be clearly thinner than that rounding, or set the rounding to 0 first. A body with a pocket - a block with a hole that does not go all the way through, made by grouping a box with a raised hole - can be hollowed too, with the top open: the walls round the pocket are hollowed as well, so a ring of cavity stays between the outer wall and the pocket, open at the top, and a thin cavity lies under the pocket's floor. Bodies that end in a point, such as a cone or a revolved triangle, have no flat face on top that could stay open. A fully closed cavity does not work there either, because a point cannot be offset inwards: even with a 1 mm wall you get the message that the walls cannot be this thick. Draw the wall into the profile before revolving instead: duplicate the outline, scale the copy down evenly, put it in the middle of the large outline and cut the large one with it, then revolve the whole (chapter Sketches, section Revolve). The distance between the two outlines is the wall thickness. If you resize a hollowed body later, layerling hollows it again at the new size right away. The wall stays as thick as you chose, round bodies included. A cylinder you pull further one way than the other becomes an ellipse. Fillets and chamfers you laid on it after the hollowing go on again at the same edges. Tip: With a 0.4 mm nozzle, 1.2 to 2 mm of wall is a good start: thin enough to save material, thick enough for a sturdy part.

h: A lid for an open body
t: 「ふた」 makes the lid for a body that is open at the top: a box you hollowed with its top open, a pot, a tray. Select the body and click 「ふた」. In the window you choose the kind: 「差しこむ」: a plate as large as the body with a lip below it that goes into the opening. 「かぶせる」: a plate a wall wider than the body with a rim below it that goes over the outside. 「Both sides」: a plate a wall wider than the body with both: a lip into the opening and a rim over the outside. The body's wall sits in a groove between them, like on a food container. 「平ら」: only the plate, to lay on top or glue on. 「Screw on」: a cap that screws on like a jar's lid, for a round body; more about it below. 「Screw in」: a plate with a threaded plug that screws into the opening of a round body; more about it below. 「Bayonet」: a twist lock for a round body, a cap pushed down over lugs and turned; more about it below. 「Slide-in」: a plate that slides into a box through one wall, like a wooden pencil box's lid; more about it below. Then you set the 「ふたの厚さ」, the 「はまり具合」 (the 「片側のすき間」 between lid and body: 0.1 mm tight, 0.2 mm normal, 0.3 mm loose, or any value up to 1 mm) and how deep the lip or rim reaches down and how thick its wall is. Click 「ふたを作る」: the lid lies beside the body, turned over with its plate down, so it prints without support. The body stays as it is. The lid follows any outline, round or angular, because it is taken from the body itself just below its rim. A body without an opening at the top only gets a flat lid; for the others, hollow it with the top open first. For a body that is an exact CAD body, such as a rounded box hollowed with Hollow, the lid is one too, with round corners that stay round: round or chamfer its edges with the edge tool like any other. Other bodies, and lids with posts for the magnets, get a lid made of triangles. Tip: How tight a lid sits depends on the printer. Print a small box with its lid first; if the lid is too tight, take the next looser fit. Tick 「Magnets in the corners」 and the lid holds by four round magnets instead of a tight fit. Pick a 「Magnet」 (6 × 2, 8 × 3 or 10 × 3 mm) or set its 「Magnet diameter」 and 「Magnet height」, and the 「Play round the magnet」: 0.1 mm to press the magnets in, 0.2 to 0.3 mm to glue them. Layerling cuts a pocket into each corner of the body's rim and one facing it into the lid's plate, a little deeper than the magnet, so it never stands proud. Where the wall is too thin for a pocket, a post fills the corner from the bottom up to the rim, and the lid's lip goes round it. The body is grouped with its pockets and posts: ungroup it and you have it back as it was. The plate must be at least the magnet's height plus 0.8 mm thick; switching the magnets on makes it so. Tick 「Hinge」 and the lid swings open about a pin along a straight side of the body: the back, or the side you pick under 「Hinge side」 (as in the starting view, where the back faces away from you). Knuckles take turns along it, the outer ones on the body and those between on the lid, 「Hinge clearance」 apart, and a hole for the pin goes through them all: with a 「Pin diameter」 of 1.75 mm a piece of filament is the pin; tick 「Print the pin too」 for a thicker one printed apart. The pin sits tight in the body's part of the hinge, so a piece of filament pressed in stays put, and turns in the lid's: 「Pin play (per side)」 is its room there on each side, 0.2 mm to begin with; give it more if the lid turns stiffly. In the body's part a printed pin has 0.15 mm on each side, as it comes out at its full width: it still sits firmly, but it can be pressed in. The body's knuckles stand on a 45° slope, so the body prints upright without support; the lid's are flush with its top, so it still prints turned over. 「Knuckles (0 = automatic)」 at 0 gives about one knuckle per 10 mm. A hinge goes with a lid that pushes in or a flat one; a rim round the outside would hit the back wall as it opens. On a round side, a pot or a tube, the hinge runs where the wall stays within a knuckle's radius of the hinge's line, and the body's knuckles stand on a small block that reaches in to the wall. 「Teardrop pin holes (no droop when printed)」 (on to start with) gives the pin's holes a point on top as each part is printed, so they do not droop; a printed pin lies on a small flat. Under 「Hinge type」, 「Flush」 puts the knuckles into the wall instead of behind it: the box keeps its size, each part is notched round the other's knuckles, and the lid opens to about 140°. 「Pivot pins」 makes a lid that lies in the opening on a small ledge and turns on two pins through the side walls, to about 95°; the box keeps its size there too. Both need a straight side and go without magnets. For a 「Flush」 hinge, tick 「End plugs」 to close the pin's hole at both ends, so the pin stays hidden and cannot slide out. The last 4 mm of the hole at each end are then square, standing on a corner so that they too have a point on top and print without drooping, and just large enough for the pin to pass: push the pin in first, then press a plug into each end. The square plugs cannot turn and sit as tight as the pin does in the body; each is cut flush with the outside of the box, rounded corners included (on such a box the hinge runs on into the corners, with plugs or without). They come out beside the lid, lying on a flat side. The pin is shorter by them, and the status bar says how long. Tip: Press the magnets into the body first. Then set one more magnet on each of them, where it snaps on the right way round, and press the lid down onto them (with a drop of glue in its pockets if they are loose): each magnet goes into the lid facing its partner, so they attract. Tick 「Click bumps」 and the lid clicks shut: small round bumps on the outside of its lip (on a lid that goes over the top, on the inside of its rim) snap into dimples that Layerling cuts into the body's wall at the same places, one in the middle of each straight side of 12 mm or more, two on a side over 80 mm, four round a round opening, and none on the hinge's side. 「Bump height」 is how far each bump reaches into the wall, 0.4 mm to begin with: less for a small box or a stiff lip, more for a firmer click. Under 「Handle」, 「Pull tab」 gives the plate a tab 6 mm out from its front edge (or the edge opposite the hinge), as thick as the plate, so the lid still prints turned over, and 「Finger notch」 cuts a recess for a finger into the body's front wall just below the lid's edge, always leaving 0.8 mm of the wall; neither goes with a pivot lid, nor do the bumps with a flat one. Pick 「Screw on」 and the lid screws on like a jar's: the body gets a thread on the outside of its top, and the cap the same thread inside its rim. This needs a round body, such as a cylinder, a tube or a round pot hollowed with its top open, with a wall at least 0.8 mm thick; a box or an oval is refused. A rim that is rounded or chamfered, as on a vessel revolved from a line with round ends, can stay as it is, for this lid and for 「Bayonet」 below: the thread or the lugs go on the straight wall under the rounding, and the cap reaches over it. The thread is added to the outside of the wall rather than cut into it, so even a thin wall keeps its strength, and it is grouped with the body: ungroup it and you have the body back as it was. 「Thread pitch」 is how far the thread climbs in one turn, 3 mm to begin with, as on a jar; the thread is three tenths of that deep (at most 1.5 mm), its flanks at 45°, so the body prints upright and the cap on its plate, both without support. 「Turns」 is how many times it goes round, and with the pitch how far the cap's rim reaches down. The 「片側のすき間」 is the thread's room on each side, measured across the radius as for a nut; if the cap turns stiffly, take a looser fit. Turn the cap clockwise to close it. Cap and thread are made of triangles, and magnets, a hinge, click bumps and a handle do not go with a screw lid. Under 「Thread」 you can pick, instead of 「Custom」, the thread of a standard bottle or jar: PCO 1881 is the 28 mm neck of most water and soft-drink bottles, PCO 1810 the older one with a taller thread, GL 45 the thread of laboratory bottles (DIN 168), Mason 70 and Mason 86 the regular and the wide mouth of mason jars. The cap is then made to the standard, so it fits such a bottle or jar from the shop; the standard sets the pitch and how far the cap reaches down, and the 「片側のすき間」 is the room all round its thread. The body gets the neck's thread only if its top is that neck: round, and as wide as the neck under its thread, which the window tells you (24.94 mm for PCO 1881); a cap from the shop then fits the body too. Any other body stays as it is and only the cap is made, as the status bar says. To make a cap for a bottle you have, select a cylinder about as wide as its neck, click 「ふた」, and pick 「Screw on」 and the bottle's thread. A standard's flanks are steeper than the 45° of the custom thread, so the thread's underside on the body and the ridges inside the cap hang over more as they print; they are only about a millimetre deep, but print one cap first to see how your printer manages them. The thread of mason jars has no published drawing, and its sizes are measured ones: try the cap on your jar. Before you click 「ふたを作る」, the window measures your body's top and says whether it is the neck: how wide it is, how wide the neck must be under the thread, and whether the body gets the thread or only the cap is made. If it is not the neck and the body is a cylinder, a tube or a hollowed cylinder standing upright, 「Fit the body to the neck」 makes it as wide as the neck, in the middle of what counts (65.85 mm for Mason 70), and keeps its height; a hollowed body keeps its walls as thick as they were. 「ふたを作る」 then gives it the neck's thread, and one undo takes the fitting back. For any other body, such as a group or an imported mesh, the window says how wide to make its top. Pick 「Screw in」 and the thread goes the other way round, for a pen holder, say, whose outside should stay smooth: the body gets the thread inside its opening, like a nut, and the lid is a plate as large as the body with a plug below it that has the same thread and screws in until the plate rests on the rim. The body and its opening must both be round, with the same middle, such as a cylinder, a tube or a round pot hollowed with its top open, with a wall at least 0.8 mm thick; a box, an oval or a square opening is refused, and so is an opening too narrow or not deep enough for the plug. Here too the thread is added to the wall rather than cut into it: the wall keeps its strength, the outside stays as it was, and the opening is only the thread's depth narrower near the top. 「Thread pitch」, 「Turns」 and the 「片側のすき間」 work as for a screw lid; pitch and turns also set how far the plug reaches down. The plug is hollow, a ring with a 「Plug wall」 of 1.6 mm to begin with (0.8 mm at least), and stays solid where the opening leaves no room for a hole. The body prints upright and the lid on its plate with the plug standing up, both without support. Turn the lid clockwise to close it. As with a screw lid, lid and thread are made of triangles, and magnets, a hinge, click bumps and a handle do not go with it. Pick 「Bayonet」 for a twist lock, as a light bulb sits in its socket, to join the sections of a lamp or close a round box: the body gets lugs standing out of the outside of its top (「Lugs」: three to begin with, two to four), and the cap an L-shaped slot inside its rim for each. Set the cap on with its slots over the lugs, push it down and turn it clockwise until it clicks, 40° with three lugs (45° with two, 30° with four): a ledge in the cap then lies under each lug and holds it down, and a stop ends the turn. 「Turn (0 = automatic)」 lets you set the turn yourself, up to a quarter turn of 90°, for example for a cap with two lugs that goes on with a 90° twist; at 0 it is the turn the lugs give. Each lug's slot, its turn and a stop before the next slot must fit round the body: with more lugs or on a small body, a turn that does not fit is held to what fits, and the status bar says so. Two lugs reach 90° on all but the smallest bodies; four turn about 65° at most on a body 40 to 80 mm across. Like a screw lid it needs a round body with a wall at least 0.8 mm thick, and the lugs are grouped with the body. They are sized from its diameter, standing a fortieth of it out of the wall (1.2 to 2.5 mm); their undersides and the ledge slope at 45°, so the body prints upright and the cap on its plate, both without support. 「外ぶちの深さ」 is how far the cap reaches down, 8 mm to begin with; below the lugs it guides the cap along the wall. The 「片側のすき間」 is the room round the lugs and along the wall, and starts from your printer's play once you have measured it; 「Gap in height」 is the room above the ledge, how far the locked cap can lift, 0.3 mm to begin with. 「Detent height」 is how far a small rib behind each locked lug reaches into its way: the lug clicks past it, so the cap does not turn back by itself. Take less if the cap turns too hard, 0 for none. To open it, turn the cap back and lift it off. Cap and lugs are made of triangles, and magnets, a hinge, click bumps and a handle do not go with a bayonet lid. Tick 「Tether」 with a screw or bayonet lid and the cap stays with the body when it is open, as on a drinks bottle. The tether is one part, lying flat beside the cap: two open rings joined by a strap. The larger ring snaps onto the cap from below and sits under a collar round its top, held there by a bead. The smaller one goes round the body just below the cap, on a bead the body gets there, and the thread or the lugs above keep it on: open it a little and push it on over them, or from below over the bead. Both rings turn freely, so the cap still turns on and off, and the strap is long enough for the open cap to hang beside the neck. Print the tether in PETG or TPU; in PLA it takes only a few bends. The beads slope at 45°, so cap and body still print without support, and the rings keep the 「片側のすき間」 round what they turn on. The tether needs a few millimetres of the body below the cap, round and as wide as at the top, and a cap rim about 4 mm deep; where that is missing, the tool says so. Screw lids and bayonet lids can be flip-tops, as on a bottle of shampoo or ketchup: tick 「Flip-top」 and the cap's plate gets a round opening in its middle (「Opening」: its diameter, 8 mm to begin with) with a flap in it that closes it, flush with the top. The cap stays on, and you open only the flap. A cap prints on its plate, so a flap folded over from beside it would lie upside down, its plug against the bed; that is why the flap is printed in the opening itself, the 「片側のすき間」 all round it, and is its own plug. Its edge narrows at 45° just below the top, so it rests on the plate and cannot be pushed in, and at the front a catch reaches under the edge of the opening, so it clicks shut. At its straight back a strip 0.4 mm thick and 3 mm long, lying flat on the bed, joins it to the plate and bends as its hinge, so the flap never comes off; under the strip, flap and plate lean towards each other in a V. Nothing slopes more than 45°, and the cap prints in one piece without support. To open the flap, put a fingernail in the groove across it and lift; to close it, press it down until it clicks. Print a flip-top in PETG or PP: in PLA the strip breaks after a few bends. The plate must be at least 1.8 mm thick (with a gap of 0.2 mm), and the opening and its hinge have to fit inside the body's opening; an opening too large is refused with the largest that fits. Screw caps and bayonet caps can have their top rim rounded or chamfered: under 「Top edge」 pick 「Rounded」 or 「Chamfer」 and set 「Edge size」, 1 mm to begin with, at most as much as the plate is thick. The edge is made with the cap, because afterwards cap and thread are one mesh with far too many triangles for the edge tool. The cap prints turned over, so this edge lies on the bed: a chamfer prints cleanly, and a rounding of 1 or 2 mm does too. Pick 「Slide-in」 for a lid that slides in like a wooden pencil box's: a plate in the opening, its top flush with the rim, whose edges run in grooves in three walls. The fourth wall, the one picked under 「Slides in from」 (the front to begin with, as in the starting view), is cut down to the lid's underside where the lid passes, so it slides in over that wall, and the lid's end fills the cut, flush with the wall's outside. A box set down turned on the workplane takes one too: the wall picked is then the one facing most nearly that way. This needs a box with upright, straight walls, rounded corners included; a round body is refused. The grooves go as deep as the 「ふたの厚さ」 allows, a little under 1 mm for a 2 mm lid and up to 1.5 mm for a thicker one, always leaving 0.8 mm of the wall behind them; their tops slope at 45°, so the box prints upright and the lid on its top, both without support. If the walls or the lid are too thin for the grooves, the window says how thick they must be. The 「片側のすき間」 is the lid's play in the grooves on each side; if it slides stiffly, take a looser fit. Walls inside the box are cut down under the lid too. Tick 「Click bumps」 and a small bump under the lid's end clicks past the cut wall, so the lid does not slide out by itself; 「Bump height」 is how far it reaches below the wall's top. Under 「Handle」, 「Finger notch」 gives the lid four grooves across its top near that end, for your thumb, and 「Pull tab」 a pull tab there. The grooves and the cut are grouped with the box as a hole: ungroup it and you have the box back as it was. Magnets and a hinge do not go with a slide-in lid. To sink the lid below the rim, set 「Frame above the lid」 (0 to begin with). The lid and its grooves then sit that much lower, and the walls keep their full height above them, a frame round the lid. The wall it slides in through is then not cut down either: it keeps its full height, with a slot through it where the lid passes, and the lid's end fills the slot, flush with the outside. Above the lid the slot leaves the same play as at its sides (「片側のすき間」), and with 「Click bumps」 the bump's height more, so the lid can bow up over its bump on the way out; at least 1 mm of the wall must stay above it, and a lower frame is refused with the frame needed (1.2 mm with a gap of 0.2 mm). The box still prints upright: the slot's top is the one place printed over air, a short, level bridge across the lid's width, which most printers bridge without support. The thumb grooves then sit just behind that wall, and a pull tab stands out of the slot.

h: A cable channel through a body
t: 「Cable channel」 runs a round tunnel through a body for a cable or an LED lead, from where it goes in to where it comes out, and finds the way itself. Select the body and click 「Cable channel」, then click on the body where the cable goes in (「Entry」) and where it comes out (「Exit」). The way starts and ends straight along the surface, runs straight where it can and bends where it must, never tighter than 「Smallest bend」, and keeps as far from the outside as it can, never closer than 「Least wall」. A cable pushes through a bend of about five times its diameter; 「Diameter」 is the channel's own. While the panel is open the body is seen through, with the channel inside it and a mark on each end. The panel says how long the channel is, its tightest bend and its thinnest wall, and in red when a bend or the wall had to be smaller than asked; a smaller value for 「Smallest bend」 or another entry or exit helps then. 「Set again」 moves an end. 「Make channel」 cuts the channel in: it becomes a 「曲がりパイプ」 as a hole, grouped with the body, so the body stays exact, and after ungrouping the tube can still be changed. A bent tube has at most eleven bends; a way that needs more asks for another entry or exit.

Every face of a body can be moved by the same distance, out or in. That is what a press fit, a lid or a snap joint needs: a gap of 0.1 to 0.3 mm all round while the features stay where they are, which scaling cannot give you. Select one body and click 「オフセット」, or right-click the body and choose it there. Choose 「拡大」 or 「縮小」 and set the 「距離」. The 「外側の角」 decide the outer corners: rounded keeps the offset surface round there, sharp lets the faces run on until they meet. Tick 「元を残し、オフセットしたボディを穴として追加」 to keep the part as it is and get the grown body as a copy that already is a hole. Group that hole with the mating part and it cuts exactly the clearance you chose. Click 「オフセット」. Tick 「側面のみ：平らな上面と底面は高さを保つ」 when only the outline should grow or shrink: the sides move by the distance, while every flat top and bottom stays at its height. A sign gets a border all round, a base gets wider, and the body does not get taller. On a stepped body each step keeps its own height. A text that is offset through its outlines keeps its height then too. Without the tick the body itself is offset. It becomes a fixed exact body, like after a chamfer: the list at the top of the tool window takes the offset back, and 「編集」 opens the tool again with the old distance. Only bodies that are exact CAD bodies can be offset - boxes, cylinders and the other shapes, groups of them, imported STEP parts. A body that is only a triangle mesh, such as many STL imports, often cannot be. A distance that is too big for the body, for example a shrink beyond its thinnest wall, is refused. A text whose letters the kernel cannot offset as a body - in some fonts an A, B, M, N, W or 9 - is offset through its outlines instead: it gets the fill 「太らせる（マルチカラープリントの土台）」 by the distance (narrower when it shrinks) and grows by as much at the top and the bottom. It stays a text you can go on editing. This works for a text with filled letters and no rounding; one that already has a fill mode is refused as before.

A fillet in the way, a hole in the wrong place, a boss you no longer need: 「面を削除」 takes it off the body again, without building the body anew. Select the body and click 「面を削除」, or right-click the body and pick it from the menu. Click every face of what should go: the faces of a rounded edge, the wall of a hole, the side and the top of a boss. A picked face lights up; another click takes it out again. The tool window counts the faces. Click 「削除」 or press Delete. Esc closes the tool without changing anything. The faces around the deleted ones grow until the gap is closed. A box with rounded top edges gets its sharp edges back, a hole is filled, a boss is gone. The body stays exact, so it can be filleted and chamfered again and the STEP export keeps its true faces. Ctrl+Z takes the deletion back in one step. It is also listed under 「エッジ処理を元に戻す」 with the fillets and chamfers, where 「元に戻す」 takes it back; there is no 「編集」 for it. On a group, the result is a single body, as with an edge treatment. Pick all the faces of what should go, and only those. If the faces around them cannot close the gap, layerling says so and nothing changes: a main side of a box, for example, has no neighbour that could take its place. Deleting only the floor of a pocket turns it into a hole straight through, because the walls of the pocket run on to the other side. 「面を削除」 needs exact faces: it works on parts imported as STEP and on layerling's shapes. Whatever layerling keeps as a mesh has none: an imported STL, OBJ or 3MF, a split, wrapped or simplified body, or a very detailed shape such as a long text. Import a part as STEP if you can. On a detailed imported part, a few faces can be too much for the CAD kernel: after 45 seconds the deletion is stopped and nothing changes. A body resized after an edge treatment while keeping its edge size has no exact faces at its new size until the resize is taken back. An imported mesh made exact with 「Make exact」 can keep hair-thin faces where the file's triangles were bad, between faces that lie in one plane, so that one side comes out as strips that cannot be deleted on their own. Such a thin face, too narrow to click, goes with a picked face when it touches it and leads on to another face in the picked face's plane, together with the thin faces joined to it that touch a face in that plane too; the tool window counts them as taken along.

Draw a flat outline, round or chamfer its corners and pull or spin it into a body. Not everything can be put together from basic shapes. For parts with a contour of their own, such as a bracket, a tooth profile or a vase, you first draw the outline and then make a body from it. That is what sketch mode is for.

At the top, switch from 「3Dエディター」 to 「スケッチ」. In the 「作成」 group of the ribbon, three buttons stand side by side for what the outline should become: 「スケッチを押し出し」: The outline is pulled upward, like a cookie cutter. 「スケッチを回転」: The outline is spun about an axis, as on a lathe. That gives vases, cups, cones and everything round. 「スケッチをスイープ」: The outline is pulled along a path: a cable channel that turns a corner, a conduit, a ring round a shape. See Sweeping along a path below. The editor then shows a sheet with a grid. That is your drawing surface. The sketch lies on the workplane. To draw on a face of a body, for an outline that should start higher up, say, first put the workplane on that face with W (see View and workplane), then start the sketch.

The ribbon in sketch mode is divided into areas. Below, each tool has a card of its own: what you do, one step to a line, and after an arrow what happens then. The key on the right of a card picks the tool.

直線1 Click points one after another. Hold Shift to snap the new line in 15° steps, horizontal and vertical included. The length and angle of the new line show at the pointer. To type how long it should be, see Lines by numbers. Every point you click lands on the snap grid set under 「スナップグリッド」. With Shift held the 15° step comes first: the length still goes in grid steps, but the end can lie between the grid lines. 円弧 Click the two ends of the arc. Click a third point the arc runs through. Until that third click a preview follows the pointer, and the message names the radius. An end clicked on an existing point joins it, so an arc can close an outline. Esc drops the points clicked so far and goes back to 「選択」. Once drawn, the arc is ordinary geometry made of points and curves: move, cut or erase it like any other line. ベジェ曲線2 Click a point and drag in the direction the line should carry on, as with the pen tool in Illustrator or Inkscape. The further you drag, the more it bends. The stretch to the new point bends along while you drag, so you see what you get. Coming from Tinkercad and just want to click points? Take the 「スムーズ曲線」. The first stretch only bends at its start if you drag at the first point too. Just clicked, the line leaves that point straight; to bend it later, select the point with 「選択」 and drag its handle. スムーズ曲線3 Click points one after another. It lays a flowing path through the points you click. At the two ends of an open line the curve heads straight for the next point, so the first and the last stretch bend less than the others. To bend one more, select its end point with 「選択」 and drag its handle. In a closed outline every point bends alike. Closing or ending a line To close the outline, click the first point again at the end. To end the chain of lines without closing the outline, right-click without moving the pointer, or double-click the last point. A body comes only from a closed outline. Freehand5 Draw with the pen, a finger or the mouse, as on paper. When you lift it, the line becomes ordinary points: a corner where it turned sharply, smooth points in between, only as many as the shape needs, so each can be dragged afterwards. Zoom in for fine detail: the closer you look, the more closely the line follows your hand. A line that ends where it began closes into an outline that can become a body; an open one stays a line, for 「線幅」 or as a path to sweep along. Start on lines or on a template picture to trace a picture by hand. Begin or end a stroke at an open end to carry that line on, so a shape can be drawn in several strokes. The stroke does not keep to the snap grid, so that it follows your hand. A point you drag afterwards does snap to it, unless 「スナップグリッド」 is switched off. The digits pick a tool as long as no line is being drawn; while one is, they are its length (see below). With 「選択」 and lines or points selected, the same keys change them instead: 1 makes lines straight and points corners, 2 turns lines into curves and 3 makes points smooth. With nothing selected they pick the tool as before.

スケッチシェイプを追加 Pick a ready-made outline: 「長方形」, 「円」, 「楕円」, 「半円」, 「扇形」, 「ボルト円」 (a disc with holes), 「三角形」, 「六角形」, a 「多角形」 or a 「星形」. Click it to put it at the origin of the sketch, or drag it from the menu to where you want it. At the bottom of the menu, 「辺数／頂点数」 sets the number of sides of the polygon and of points of the star, and 「星形の内側のサイズ」 how deep the star's valleys reach in towards the middle (10 to 90 percent of the outer radius). Both apply to the next shape you add. Like every sketch shape they are ordinary corner points afterwards, so you can move, round or chamfer them one by one. The rectangle starts with the width and depth set for the box under 「シェイプの初期値」 in the settings, the circle and the ellipse with the width of the cylinder there; without a default of your own, and for the other shapes, they start 20 mm across. Overlapping outlines Push two closed outlines over each other. They stay two bodies, which merge in the 3D editor; the overlap is not a hole. Moving does not join the lines where they cross, so you can pull the shapes apart again. Draw a line across others instead, and layerling puts a point at every crossing. A hole only comes from an outline lying wholly inside another.

選択 Click a point or a line and drag it to move it. Click inside a closed outline to select the whole outline; inside a hole it picks the hole. You can drag or resize it straight away. Hold Shift and click to add a point or line to the selection or take it away again, so you can move several together. Drag a box over empty space to select everything in it. Drag a line to move it by its two ends, or all of the selection if it is part of one. The arrow keys move the selection by one grid step, Shift with them by a larger one. Hold Shift while you drag to keep the move on one axis. The frame round the selection Drag a corner handle to change width and height together; hold Shift to keep the proportions. Drag a side handle to change one direction only. Click the width or height pill to type a new size, also as a sum ("60+12.5") or in percent ("150%"). Drag the curved arrows beyond the corners to turn the whole selection about its middle. The figure over the pointer shows the angle; with Shift held it moves in steps of 15°. While you turn, a ring appears: with the pointer inside it the turn snaps to 22.5°, outside it goes in whole degrees, whatever the grid. R turns a whole closed outline by 45° at each press. The bar above the sketch 「比率を保つ」 keeps the proportions without Shift: the corners and sides then stretch both ways alike, and a typed width or height changes the other one too. layerling remembers the switch. The X and Y fields show where the middle of the selection lies, in mm from the sketch's origin. Type a value to move it there, for a hole exactly 12 mm from the middle, say. Y counts upwards, as in the 3D editor. With two or more outlines selected, the bar lines them up: left, centred or right, and top, centred or bottom, on the frame round all of them. Each outline moves as a whole and keeps its shape; centred both ways, two circles become a ring. Locking an outlineCtrl+L Click 「ロック」 in the bar to lock the selected outline, like a locked body in the 3D editor. It can no longer be moved, resized, turned or changed. Its lines turn paler, its points grey, and the frame's handles turn grey and no longer respond. Lines may still start at its corners. When outlines are lined up, a locked one stays where it is and the others line up on it. To free it, click the padlock in its corner while it is selected, or click 「ロック解除」. 点を追加または削除4 Click a section to add a point. Click a point to remove it. layerling joins its two neighbours, so the outline stays closed. 消去 Click a point or a line to take it away. Drag a window over several to take away everything inside it. With something selected, the button erases the selection. To get rid of only a piece of a circle, for a rounded corner say, click exactly that piece of arc between two points. The rest stays. Closing a gap Drag one open end onto the other, for example after erasing one side of a hexagon. It snaps there and the two become one point, so the outline is closed again. At a crossing, such as where a line cuts a circle, the sides that run straight on are joined: arc with arc, line with line, and the circle stays round. 画像を追加 Put a template picture under the sketch to trace it, see A picture as template.

Copy, paste, duplicate, delete 「コピー」, 「貼り付け」, 「複製」 and 「削除」 work on the selected points, lines and images, as in the 3D editor; Ctrl+X cuts. Pasted and duplicated geometry lands next to the original with a 10 mm gap, on a free spot where it touches no existing line, so it never gets joined to what is already there. It stays selected, so you can drag it straight into place. 「スケッチを元に戻す」 and 「スケッチをやり直す」 take a step back and forward again.

メモN Click 「メモ」 under 「スケッチ表示の操作」, then click where the note should go: anywhere, on a line too. Drag the pin to move it; a click on the pin folds the card away. The notes of a sketch belong to its body: in the 3D view they sit on top of an extruded or swept body and on the drawn profile of a revolved one, and they move with it. Opening the sketch again shows all of the body's notes, those placed in 3D too. 「スケッチを元に戻す」 takes back a note like a line, and 「キャンセル」 discards what changed in the notes. More in the chapter Measuring and notes.

Moving the view Pan with the middle mouse button, or with Shift or Ctrl plus the right mouse button, as in the 3D editor. With nothing selected, Ctrl and the arrow keys slide it too: a tenth of the view a press, half with Shift as well; the sketch moves the way they point. Home fits the whole sketch in the view, F zooms to the selection (with nothing selected, to the whole sketch), and + and − zoom in and out, as in the 3D editor. With nothing selected, double-click an empty spot to slide it to the middle of the view. 「作業平面をダブルクリックするとそこがビューの中央になる」 in the settings switches the double-click off. Dimensions Click a line or a point. The sketch shows the length of the line, or for a point the lengths of the lines that meet there. 「寸法を表示」 on the sketch toolbar hides and shows these dimensions when they get in the way, for example while shaping curves. The 「メジャー」 on the sketch toolbar measures the distance between two points; it keeps working with the dimensions hidden. An L-shaped outline. At the selected corner point, top left, the lengths of the two lines are shown in millimetres, and the angle between them in degrees. Typing a length Click the dimension pill of a straight line and type the length in millimetres. Enter applies it, Esc cancels. The line keeps its direction, its start point stays where it is, and the lines at the other end follow. With an end point selected, that one moves. Alt+Enter grows the line to both sides around its middle instead. On curves the pill only shows the length.

Once you have set the first point with 「直線」 or 「スムーズ曲線」, just type a number: two fields open next to the line, 「長さ」 in millimetres and 「角度」 in degrees. < or Tab moves to the angle, so "50<30" gives a line 50 mm long at 30°, as in AutoCAD. Enter sets the point, and you can type the next line straight away; Esc closes the fields without ending the line chain. The angle counts counterclockwise from the right: 0° to the right, 90° up, 180° to the left, 270° down. Leave it empty and the line follows the pointer, so you give only the length and show the direction with the mouse. Sums like "40+12.5" work in both fields. If the point would land off the plate, the field says so and waits for another value.

Select a straight line and click 「線を曲げる」 in the bar that appears: the side bows out into a curve, as in Tinkercad, and shows its two handles. Drag them to shape the curve; the further out a handle stands, the stronger the bend. Under the pointer a handle turns orange, and it also catches a click just beside it, so a template image underneath does not move by mistake. 「直線にする」 makes the side straight again. A point you select can be made round with 「スムーズ曲線」: it gets handles of its own and the lines next to it become curves. With three or more points selected, 「点を通る曲線」 in the bar lays one flowing curve from the first of them to the last, through every point in between, the way the 「スムーズ曲線」 tool draws one; the lines beyond the two ends stay as they are. Other programs call this "Fit curve" or "Fit point spline". The two differ: 「線を曲げる」 bends each selected side on its own and keeps the corners between them, for an arch on one side; 「点を通る曲線」 runs one curve through the points with no corners left, for smoothing a jagged traced edge. Click a handle and it lights up: the arrow keys then move it by one grid step, with Shift by a larger step, so you can set a curve precisely. Values can be typed too. A selected point shows 「X」 and 「Y」 in the bar: where it lies, in mm from the sketch's origin, with Y counting up. Click a handle and the bar shows 「ハンドル X」 and 「ハンドル Y」 instead: where the handle lies from its own point. On a smooth point the opposite handle turns along. Give the matching handle on the other side the same Y and the X with the opposite sign, and the curve comes out exactly mirrored; 「ミラー」 mirrors a whole half at once. The bottom side of the L-shaped outline bent into a curve, with its two handles at the ends.

Click a corner point where two straight lines meet: next to the lengths, layerling shows the angle between them in degrees, with a small arc. On a closed outline it is the angle inside the shape, so a dent reads above 180°. Click the value and type a new angle. One of the two lines then turns about the corner and keeps its length, and the other stays where it is. The line that turns is drawn dashed; Tab switches to the other one, Enter applies and Esc cancels. What hangs at the far end of the turned line goes with it. A locked point stays where it is, and a typed value works round it: a length moves the free end of the line, and an angle turns the line whose far end is free. A single point can be locked as well: select it and press Ctrl+L. That way you can make an outline exact one corner after the other: lock a corner, type the length and the angle of the next line, lock its end, and go on. Moving a point changes three angles: at the point itself and at the two neighbouring corners at the far ends of its lines. So layerling shows those two as well, and each can be clicked and typed. That way you set, say, the bottom left corner to 75.5° while the top left point, which moves for it, is selected. You can calculate here too, e.g. "90-14.5". A corner shows no angle where a curve meets it, or where more than two lines meet. The 「寸法を表示」 button on the sketch toolbar hides the angle together with the lengths.

Click a corner point and choose 「角をフィレット」 or 「角を面取り」. A small field appears for the 「半径」 or the 「距離」. Enter the size and confirm with the check mark. This works for corners between two straight lines. Several corners at once work too: select them with Shift and a click each, or pull a frame round them, and choose 「角をフィレット」 or 「角を面取り」 from the bar that appears. All of them get the same radius or distance. Where two selected corners share a side, each takes at most 45 % of it, so a rectangle rounded all round comes out alike at every corner. Points that are not a corner between two straight lines are left out, and the message says how many. A frame round a whole shape, or a click inside it, selects its corners and its lines together, and the bar then offers 「線を曲げる」 and 「直線にする」 for all the selected lines next to the corner tools. The corner at the top left is rounded with a 12 mm radius.

Select points and lines (click, Shift and click, or pull a frame round them) and click 「ミラー」 in the bar. Then choose the axis: 「左右」 mirrors across the vertical axis through the middle of the plate, 「上下」 across the horizontal one, and 「線をはさんで」 across a straight line of the sketch that you click next. The copy is added on the other side and the original stays; nothing is linked, so you can change either on its own. Points that lie on the axis are shared, so a half outline whose ends sit on the axis becomes one closed outline: draw half of a bracket, select it, mirror it and make the body. A construction line makes a good axis. Esc cancels.

A construction line helps you place points without becoming part of the body. It is drawn dashed and never counts as outline: you can pull it as far beyond the shape as you like and the body does not grow. Switch on 「補助線」 in the 「描画」 group. New lines, those typed by measure too, are then construction lines. The button switches back to normal lines. A line you have drawn already becomes a construction line when you click it and choose 「補助線」. 「線にする」 makes it a normal line again. New points snap to where a construction line crosses another line, a blue ring shows it, and to the ends of the construction line. That is how you put a corner on a middle, at a fixed distance from an edge or on a crossing, without calculating. New points also snap to the middle of every straight line of the sketch, to the centre of every circle and rounded corner, and to the middles of the sides of a body shown underneath (#624). A point that is being dragged ignores the middle of its own lines. A selection you drag snaps with its middle (#1236): the centre of a circle or the middle of a rectangle lands on the ends, corners and middles of the other lines, on the centres of circles, where construction lines cross and on the corners of a body underneath; a blue ring shows where. A shape dragged in from 「スケッチシェイプを追加」 lands with its middle on these points too. Hold Alt to keep to the grid only. 「まん中から線を引く」 in the 「描画」 group draws a line from its middle: click the middle first, then the end, and the line runs the same length to the other side. The middle becomes a point of its own. Click the button again to draw normal lines. A construction line does not cut the outline apart where it crosses it. When revolving it may lie to the right of the axis too.

Click 「スケッチを完了」. The outline stands as a body on the workplane. In its settings you change the height, the colour and everything else as with any other shape. When you resize it, layerling builds it again from the sketch a moment later, and the sketch grows with it. So it stays an exact body that takes chamfers and fillets, and the next time you edit it the sketch has the size the body has. If the workplane lies on the side of a body, you draw the way you look at that side: up in the sketch is up on the finished body too. The faint outline of the body in the sketch view shows where it stands. If the workplane cuts through a body, the sketch view shows the outline of that cut instead, so a hollow body appears as a ring and you can line the sketch up with its walls. A point you set or drag close to a corner of these outlines snaps exactly onto it; a small blue ring shows it. That way you take edges of other bodies into the sketch, even when the workplane does not lie exactly on them. To trace round existing work, switch on 「透けて見えるパーツを表示: スケッチ平面上のすべてのエッジ」 (the layers button in the view buttons on the left): all the edges of the bodies are then drawn on the sketch plane, thin and faint, as if you looked through them, whatever height they lie at. A plane that stands upright, set on a front face for example, shows the front view this way. The choice is kept in the browser. The outline has become a body. The corner is rounded. With 「スケッチを編集」 you can return to the sketch at any time to change it. A double click on the body does the same, as in Tinkercad (a locked body stays closed); 「ダブルクリックでスケッチを開く」 in the settings switches that off. Edge treatments you already made on the body are lost, though, because the edges are created anew. A body you turned or moved in the 3D editor opens where it stands on the plate, turned as you see it there and on the plate's grid; only a tilted or mirrored body opens in its own frame. A sketch with several outlines makes one body, and outlines that overlap merge in it. To have every outline on its own, select the body and click 「パーツを分離」: each outer outline becomes a body of its own, with the holes that lie in it, and keeps the body's height, colour and place. Each part has its own sketch to edit, with the construction lines, so you can raise or lower the parts one by one and join or cut them afterwards. Edge treatments block this, as does a body stretched since: it is then taken apart as a mesh. Another kind of body from the same sketch: the badge at the top of the sketch says what it becomes, 「押し出しスケッチ」, 「回転体スケッチ」 or 「スイープスケッチ」. Click it and pick another, also while you edit an existing body: an imported SVG, which comes in extruded, becomes a vase or a knob when you switch it to 「回転体スケッチ」. An outline reaching across the axis moves left until its right edge lies on the axis, so the half cross-section of an SVG turns about its straight side; Ctrl+Z takes the move back. When you finish, the new body takes the old one's place, name and colour, its foot at the same height. Edge treatments go, as with every edit of a sketch.

When revolving, you draw half the cross-section to the left of the axis shown in the sketch. Next to it you see a 3D preview of the revolve. It shows at once what the body will look like. You can turn, shift and zoom it with the mouse; the small button in its top right corner, or a double click on it, brings back the first view. The outline must be closed, or you build an open line as a stroke, see below. At the end click 「回転を完了」. The other bodies of the design are shown from the front, in the same view as the profile, with the axis standing at the middle: draw the profile next to them or above them. The body stands where you drew it, and the horizontal line through the middle of the sketch is the ground: a profile drawn above it gives a body that stands higher, and its lowest point is the foot of the body. For a bigger radius, move the profile further from the axis, past the edge of the plate if need be: the plate grows with the sketch, its grid follows when you let go, and the minus button zooms out until all of it fits. A revolved body is an exact body, like an extruded one: it takes chamfers and fillets, and you can hollow it, for a cup or a vase. A body revolved with an older layerling is a mesh; open 「スケッチを編集」 and finish it again to make it exact. A profile that reaches across the axis cannot be built exactly and becomes a mesh, as before. Smoother round faces: 「Smoothness」. An exact revolved body is cut into small flat facets for the view, the export and the print, and on a large pot they can show on the print. Select the body and set 「Smoothness」 in the properties panel to 「Fine」 or 「Extra fine」: the round faces are cut finer, at the cost of more triangles and a slower design. A helix or a mesh revolve has 「辺の数」 for this instead. One continuous strand: 「ピッチ」. A revolve turns its outline into closed rings. Select the revolved body and give it a 「ピッチ」 above 0 in the properties panel, the distance it climbs per turn, and the outline winds up as a helix instead: one continuous strand, like filament on a spool or a coil. 「スイープ角」 then becomes 「巻き数」, up to 200; a negative number winds left-handed. Turns closer than the outline is high melt into one body, so a solid core with a fine pitch works too. A helix is built as a mesh, so fillet, chamfer and hollow do not work on it; keep 「辺の数」 low on many turns. A pitch of 0 makes rings again.

「スケッチをスイープ」 pulls an outline along a path: a cable channel that turns a corner, a conduit, a guard round a belt, a ring around a hexagon. It sits next to 「スケッチを押し出し」 and 「スケッチを回転」 in the 「作成」 group. You draw two things on the same sheet: The cross-section as a closed outline, as usual. Draw it as you would see it looking along the path from its start: across the path is the sketch's left and right, up is up on the finished body. A hollow section, a channel or a tube, is an outline with another one inside it. By default the section is centred on the path. The menu next to the mode badge at the top lets you put its left or right edge on the path instead (「道すじに合わせる：左のはし」, 「道すじに合わせる：右のはし」, seen looking along the path), so a rail can sit on one side of the line or follow the edge of a part. The body stands on the sketch plane with the lowest point of the section. The path as a 「補助線」: switch it on and draw lines or curves, one chain, open or closed (a closed chain gives a ring). The path lies flat in the sketch plane. Draw the section near the end of the path where it should start; the path starts at the end nearest to it. Then click 「スイープを完了」. A corner of straight pieces becomes a mitre, a curve stays smooth, and the section stays upright all the way. The body is exact, like an extruded one: fillet, chamfer and the STEP export work on it. If a closed outline or a path is missing, or there are several separate paths, layerling says so. With 「スケッチを編集」 you can return to the sketch and change the section or the path.

Normally the area inside a closed outline becomes the body. With 「線幅」 in the 「完了」 section you build the line itself instead, with a width you set. Tick 「線として作る」 in the stroke window; the sketch shows straight away what comes out. A closed outline becomes a frame. 「位置」 says where the wall lies: 「中央」 on the drawn line, 「内側」 within it or 「外側」 outside it. Outside is handy for a tolerance: draw the outline of a hole, a dovetail for instance, and give it a 0.2 mm stroke outside to get the gap the print needs. An open line becomes a stripe, centred on the line. 「端」 sets how its ends look: 「平ら」, 「四角」 (longer by half the width) or 「丸」. 「角」 applies to both: 「鋭角」, 「丸」 or 「斜め」. The sketch keeps the drawn line. Open it again and you go on changing line and stroke; untick the box and the area is built again. Curves are broken into short straight pieces for it. In a revolve the stroke is a thin wall: draw the wall of a vase or a cup as one open line to the left of the axis, tick 「線幅」 and set the width, and the revolve turns that band. What reaches across the axis is cut off at it.

You can set the stroke without opening the sketch too: in the properties of a sketch body, choose 「面」, 「線（外側）」, 「線（内側）」 or 「線（中央）」 under 「塗り」, with 「線の幅」 and 「角」. The body is built again straight away, where it stands. These match the fill modes of Tinkercad's SVG import: default, outer line and inner line. 「太らせる」 keeps the area filled and grows it by the line width all round, with sharp, round or bevelled corners: a base layer under a logo for a multicolour print, which the stroke outside alone would only give as a ring. 「細らせる」 does the opposite: the area stays filled and its edge moves in by the line width all round, holes included (they grow). Use both on copies of one sketch for a fit: the hole at its drawn size, the part that goes through it 「細らせる」 by 0.5 mm, or a wall inside a shape cut from the same outline. A width larger than the outline allows leaves nothing. In the sketch's stroke window the same two choices stand under 「位置」. With a line outside, inside or centred, 「刃」 makes the wall sharp on top: its top runs in to that width with a 45° chamfer on both sides, as on a cookie cutter. 0 leaves the top flat; the edge stays when you change the line width. 「シルエット（穴なし）」 leaves out every outline lying inside another: holes and whatever lies in them. Only the outer outline stays. Together with 「線（外側）」 it makes a cookie cutter: import an SVG twice, once with the silhouette as an area for the base and once with the silhouette and 1 to 2 mm of stroke outside as the wall. The switch is in the 「線幅」 window in sketch mode as well. Fillets and chamfers on the edges go when the body is built again, as when the sketch is edited.

An extruded sketch has vertical walls. A stamp, an embossing die or a punch wants slanted ones, outside and inside, with the same wall thickness all the way. Layerling has no draft angle for an extrusion, but for plain outlines the 「テーパー」 gets you there. One way that works: Draw the outline with the hole it needs and make a body of it. Duplicate the body (Ctrl+D). On the first body, switch on 「シルエット（穴なし）」, so the hole is filled, and give it a wider bottom than top with 「テーパー」. On the copy, open its sketch again and delete the outer outline, so that only the outline of the hole is left. Finish the sketch, switch the body to 「穴」 and give it a narrower bottom than top with 「テーパー」. Move the hole into the first body, where the hole was, and group the two. The walls now slope outside and inside. Taper scales the whole outline, so this is exact for plain shapes, where you can choose the sizes so the walls run parallel, and only an approximation for fine details such as lettering.

With 「画像を追加」 you put a photo or a drawing under the sketch and trace it, at any time, also before the first line. You can set its size, opacity and position. Once the picture sits right, lock it with Ctrl+L so you do not move it by accident while drawing. A locked image is out of the way: clicks go through it, so you can pick lines and points on top of it and drag a frame over them. The padlock in its corner unlocks it with one click; Alt+click selects it without unlocking it. If its settings at the right edge cover the picture, drag them away by their title bar; a double-click on it docks them again. Under 「整列」 you line up a photo that was not taken straight: 「回転」: Turn the picture about its centre, with the curved arrows beyond its corners or as a number in degrees. With Shift the arrows snap in 15° steps. Inside the ring that appears while turning they snap to 22.5°, outside it to whole degrees. 「X = 0へ」 and 「Y = 0へ」: put the picture's centre on X = 0 or Y = 0. For a revolve, X = 0 is the axis, so the picture then lies symmetric about it. 「キャリブレーション」: Its button sits at the top, right under the preview. Click two points in the picture whose distance you know, the ends of a ruler or a known diameter, and type the real distance. The picture is scaled evenly so that distance is right; the first point stays where it was. 「トリミング」: The handles on the frame now crop the picture instead of scaling it; what is cut away stays stored and comes back with 「画像全体を表示」 or when a handle is pulled out again. All four touch the reference only, never the sketch. 「トレース」, in the picture's settings, sets the points for you: it traces the outline of the shape in the picture – a silhouette, a logo, a word – and shows it in red over the picture, square points for corners, round ones for smooth points. 「Dark shape」 or 「Light shape」 picks which part of the picture is the shape, 「しきい値」 where dark turns light, 「Points」 how many points the outlines get together (fewer give smoother curves, more follow the picture more closely), 「Corner from」 from what turn a point is a corner, 「Leave out specks up to」 how small a speck is left out, and 「Keep holes」 keeps the middle of an A or an O. 「Apply」 puts the outlines into the sketch exactly where the picture lies, at its size, turn and crop, and selects them: they are ordinary points to move, curve or remove, and Ctrl+Z takes them back in one step. It works best with clear contrast; cut a photo with a busy background out first. What falls away – around the outlines, in the holes, what is cut away – the preview covers in the plate's colour, so only what stays shows of the picture. Outlines that lie so close that loose curves would cross get more points by themselves; the card says so. For a border outside or inside the outline, give the sketch body a stroke outside or inside its lines, or offset the finished body. For a photo – a toy on a white table, say – choose 「Object」 under 「Shape」: the background is the colour at the picture's edge, and everything that stands out from it becomes one outline, whatever its colours; 「しきい値」 then sets how clearly it must stand out. A colourful picture on an even background starts this way. 「Pick areas」 outlines more: click an area in the picture, a window say, and the patch of like colour round the spot is outlined (「Colour tolerance」 sets how like). Holes and clicked areas are listed under 「Holes and areas」; pointing at one shows it in the preview, ✕ takes it out, and with 「Cut out」 off it is drawn as a construction line instead of a hole. An area that reaches the picture's edge is the background and is not taken. What no threshold and no colour can tell apart – a shadow as dark as the wheels above it – 「Cut away」 takes away: click corners round it (a click on the first corner, a double click or Enter closes it), and the outline runs along the cut; it is listed as “Cut 1”. The tree beside a house, a figure before a busy background – where no colour tells the shape from the rest, the 「Magnetic lasso」 catches it: click roughly along its edge, and between two clicks the line follows the edge by itself, round its bends too; while you move, the preview already shows where it will run. A click on the first point, a double click or Enter closes it, Esc throws it away. It is listed as “Lasso 1”, with the choice 「Take in」 (the area joins the shape) or 「Cut away」 (it is taken away); every cut has the same choice. Under 「Shape」, 「Lasso only」 makes the shape only of what you catch this way – nothing else of the picture. A drawn house traced as the object, the threshold lowered for its light wall: the magnetic lasso has cut the tree away, and the eight window panes are picked as holes. The house as a body: without the tree, the windows cut through.

Key Effect Esc put the note tool down; otherwise put the tool down (back to 「選択」), then clear the selection Delete delete the selected element Ctrl+C copy the selection Ctrl+X cut the selection Ctrl+V paste Ctrl+D duplicate the selection Ctrl+Z undo Ctrl+A select every point and line Ctrl+I 「画像を追加」 Shift while drawing: snap the line in 15° steps; while dragging: keep movement on one axis digit, <, Tab, Enter while drawing: type and set the length and angle of the next line R rotate the closed sketch by 45° Ctrl+L lock or unlock the selected outline, or the template image N place a note: the next click puts it on the sketch Shift+N show or hide the notes Tip: Draw as few points as needed. An outline with a few well-placed points gives a smoother body than a tangle of many.
Raised or engraved lettering in eight typefaces or one of your own, and if you like along a circular arc, such as on a coin, a lid or a ring.

Choose 「テキスト」 in the shape library and place it. In the 「テキスト」 field on the right, type what it should say. The settings below: 「フォント」: Eight typefaces are available: Multilanguage, Sans, Serif, Script, Monospace, Rounded, Stencil (letters made of straight lines) and Japanese (Zen Maru Gothic). New text starts in Sans. Accented letters such as ä, ö, ü, é and the € sign are in every typeface, and so are kana, the common kanji and many of the rare ones in names such as 澤, 槇 and 檜: a Japanese name works in every typeface and on a name tag. The Japanese letters are fetched the first time a text needs them (the rare kanji in a second file, only when a text has one), so such a text shows question marks for a moment. They are kept on the computer afterwards, so Japanese also works offline from then on. Fonts of your own come on top, see Your own fonts below. 「文字サイズ」: How big the letters are, seen from above; 「高さ」 sets how thick they are. 「高さ」: How far the lettering stands out from the surface. 「ベベル」: Rounds the letter edges so they look softer. With 「分割数」 you decide in how many steps. 「文字のエッジ」: rounds or chamfers the top edge of the letters, as on a name tag: 「なし」, 「丸」 or 「面取り」, with the 「エッジのサイズ」 (0.4 mm to start with, at most as high as the text). It goes further than the 「ベベル」, but only as far as the strokes are wide: where a stroke is thinner than twice the size, the edge ends in a narrower top. The underside stays flat, so single letters can be glued on afterwards. While an edge is chosen it takes the place of 「ベベル」. Length: A text takes up to 250 characters. The letters keep their size and the line gets as long as it needs to be; to make it shorter, make the letters smaller. The 「文字のエッジ」 works on a text of up to 40 characters, because on a longer one it would take minutes to build. Size: You set the length and width of the line as with any shape. Drag the handles or type the dimensions. 「文字の間隔（%）」: The space between the letters on top of the one the font has, in per cent of the letter size: 0 leaves it as the font made it, above it the letters stand further apart, below it (down to -50) tighter, which a font of your own often needs. The letters keep their size and the box follows the line, on straight and on curved text. The spacing is not applied to Arabic and Hebrew, whose letters join up. 「文字を枠いっぱいに広げる」: Off at first: the letters keep their proportions and sit in the middle of the frame, so a frame pulled wider or deeper than the word needs stays larger than the letters. Switch it on and the letters are stretched to fill the whole frame in both directions: a capital can be made lower or narrower, as in Tinkercad. It is for straight text; curved text has its own letter size. 「Automatic kerning」: Moves pairs of letters that leave too much room between them, such as AY, AV, LT or To, closer, measured from the shapes of the letters, in every font, your own too. New texts start with it on; texts made before it existed have it off, so nothing moves in a saved design. The letters keep their size and the box follows. It works on straight and curved text, not on vertical text, Arabic, Hebrew or Japanese. 「文字を縦に並べる」: Stacks the letters top to bottom, each in the middle of one upright line, for a sign on a door frame or a name down a pen. The box turns upright and the letters keep their size; 「文字の間隔（%）」 sets the gap between them. On curved text the letters form a column along the left side of the circle, each one standing upright; 「右側にそわせる」 puts the column on the right side. Text is at first a single body. If you want to treat the letters individually, click 「パーツを分離」. Then every letter is a shape of its own. Several lines: A text holds one line. For a sign or a plaque with several lines, open the 「Text block」 card below the settings: type the lines under 「Lines」, choose 「Align」 (「Left」, 「Centre」 or 「Right」), 「Line gap」 and 「Next line (%)」 - at 80 % each line is a fifth smaller than the one above. The button makes every line a text of its own under the one above, in this text's font, height and fill; the first takes this text's place. Afterwards each line can get its own size, font or colour. The edges of text can be chamfered or filleted too, straight or curved, see Breaking edges and hollowing bodies. Use small sizes such as 0.2 to 0.5 mm, because the strokes of the letters are narrow.

The list under 「フォント」 draws every font in its own letters, with the words of your text, so you see how they will look before you choose. The same goes for the fonts in the window below; the fonts listed from your computer show their names in their own letters. Arrow keys and Enter work in the list, and a letter jumps to the next font that starts with it. Besides the eight built-in fonts you can use any font of your own: a font file from your computer or, in Chrome and Edge, a font installed on your computer. Choose 「自分のフォント…」 at the bottom of 「フォント」. The 「自分のフォント」 window opens. 「フォントファイルを選ぶ…」 takes a TrueType file (.ttf), an OpenType file (.otf) or a WOFF file (.woff). You can also simply drag the file into the window. On Windows the installed fonts live in the Fonts folder (C:\Windows\Fonts). The browser's file dialog hides it. Open it in Explorer instead and drag the font into the 「自分のフォント」 window. Fonts installed for you alone live in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Fonts, which the file dialog shows too. On a Mac fonts live in /Library/Fonts and ~/Library/Fonts. 「コンピューターのフォント…」 lists the fonts installed on your computer. The first time, the browser asks whether layerling may read them. The search field finds a font quickly, a click takes it. If a text is selected, it gets the new font at once. Otherwise the font shows up under 「フォント」 in the 「自分のフォント」 group, and 「使う」 in the window puts it on the selected texts. Fonts of your own work like the built-in ones: text on a circular arc, chamfers and fillets on the edges and the STEP export all work the same. Letters a font lacks are taken from Sans.

Arabic, Persian, Urdu and Hebrew are written right to left: the first letter stands on the right, and in a mixed text such as "Name عربي" only the Arabic word runs backwards, digits stay as usual. Arabic letters join their neighbours the way the script asks, and lam-alef becomes a ligature. This needs a font that has these letters; the built-in ones do not. Add one of your own, such as Arial, Tahoma or Segoe UI on Windows, or a free one such as Noto Naskh Arabic, Noto Sans Arabic or Amiri. Vowel marks sit on the letter they belong to. Text on a circular arc, outline, silhouette, layers and name tags work with it as with any other text.

Browser Choose a font file Font from the computer Chrome and Edge on a computer, the installed layerling app too yes yes, after the browser asks Firefox yes no Safari on a Mac yes no Tablet and phone yes, from the device's files no Web pages may not simply read the installed fonts. Only Chrome and Edge have a permission for it, and only on secure pages, over https as on layerling.com. When layerling runs over http, say on your own server or as a Docker install in your home network, 「コンピューターのフォント…」 is missing; drag the font over from Explorer then. In the other browsers you choose the font file from the fonts folder, with the same result. If you declined the question in Chrome or Edge, allow it again in the site settings, behind the padlock to the left of the address. layerling cannot read WOFF2 files (there is almost always a TTF or OTF version), font collections (.ttc, several fonts in one file) or colour emoji fonts. From very large fonts, such as Chinese ones, layerling takes the first 8000 characters. A variable font is read in its default setting, usually the regular weight. Some fonts, script and variable fonts above all, draw a letter from strokes that overlap. layerling merges them into one clean outline when it reads the font, so the body stays printable. Such letters are then made of very short straight pieces instead of curves; it does not show.

A font of your own stays in this browser on this computer. Another browser or another computer does not know it until you add it there too. Clearing the browser's site data clears the fonts as well. In the 「自分のフォント」 window the bin removes a font from the browser. Your designs lose nothing by it, as the next section shows.

h: Passing on designs with a font of your own
t: A design does not store the font file, only the outlines of the letters its texts use, those in earlier steps of the history included. If a text says "Hello", only H, e, l and o travel with it. That holds for every way a design is saved: in the browser, on your own server, as a .lyl file and in 「カスタムシェイプ」. So: The design opens correctly anywhere, also on a computer without the font. The texts look the same and can be moved, turned, scaled and filleted. New letters need the font. If someone without the font types a letter the design did not bring along, layerling draws it from Sans. Under 「フォント」 the font is then marked 「デザインの文字のみ」. Adding the font file brings back every letter. Exports hold geometry only. STL, 3MF, OBJ, STEP and SVG contain bodies and outlines, no font. Older layerling versions do not know fonts of one's own yet and draw such texts in Multilanguage. Licences: Fonts are protected by copyright, and their licence says what you may do with them. The embedded letter outlines are what PDF files take along from a font, and most licences allow that. Some commercial fonts, though, forbid passing on even single letters. Before you pass on or publish a design with a font of your own, check the font's licence. Free fonts such as those from Google Fonts (mostly under the SIL Open Font License) can be passed on without worry. For a printed part or an exported STL it does not matter: they hold no font any more, only geometry.

Raised: Place the text on the surface and group it with the body. It grows out as a relief. Engraved: Switch the text to 「穴」, let it reach a little into the surface and group it with the body. The letters are then engraved. For lettering on a side face, first put the workplane on that face, see View and workplane.

h: Stencils: bridges for the middle of letters
t: Cut through a plate, letters like O, A and B lose their middle: it lies loose inside the letter and falls out. 「ステンシルブリッジ」 holds it to the plate with small bridges, as on a stencil. Switch the text to 「穴」, let it reach through the plate and select both, grouped or not. Click 「ステンシルブリッジ」 in the 「変形」 group of the ribbon, right-click the selection, or find it with Ctrl+K. The bridges show in orange where they will go. Set 「ブリッジの幅」 and 「パーツごとのブリッジの数」. 「ブリッジの高さ」 starts at the plate's thickness; lower bridges sit flush with the bottom, in the middle or flush with the top of the plate, as 「位置」 says. On a spray stencil, bridges at the top leave room under them for the paint. 「作成」 groups the bridges with the plate. Each bridge is an ordinary box: open the group to move one, delete one or add one of your own. If you change the text later, select the group and click 「ステンシルブリッジ」 again; new bridges take the place of the old ones. A text that is engraved and does not go through gets no bridges, as nothing falls out there. For a laser or a plotter, the DXF and SVG export add the same bridges, see Files, saving and sharing.

A text need not be built as filled letters. 「塗り」 in the properties offers the same choice as Tinkercad: 「塗りつぶし」: the letters as they are. 「輪郭線」: a line along the outline of the letters, half inside and half outside it. 「外側の線」: a line round the outside of the letters. 「内側の線」: a line on the inside of the letters. With a line chosen, two settings appear right under the list: 「線の幅」 sets how thick the line is, 「角」 how it goes round the corners (「丸」, 「斜め」 or 「鋭角」). The rarer settings are under 「詳細」: 「シルエット（穴なし）」 leaves out the holes in O, A or e, and 「太らせる（マルチカラープリントの土台）」 keeps the letters filled and makes them thicker by the line width all round; letters that touch grow into one piece. With a line outside, a centred line or "Wider" the box of the text grows, while the letters keep their size. 「ベベル」 and 「分割数」 exist for filled letters only.

A name tag for a multicolour print is a text in layers: the letters on top, under them the same text a little wider in a second colour, at the bottom a plate without holes in a third. layerling makes it in one click: A new name tag: choose 「ネームタグ」 in the shape library and place it. It says "Name" in white letters on a red rim and a dark plate. From a text: select the text and click 「レイヤーを作る」 at the top of its settings. All settings of the tag are in the card 「ネームタグ」, at the top of the settings: 「テキスト」 and 「フォント」, fonts of your own too. The tag grows with the words. 「文字サイズ」: how tall the capital letters are, in mm. All layers follow and stay lined up. 「文字を縦に並べる」: stands the tag upright with the letters under one another, all layers along. 「レイヤー」: one row per layer, from the top down. Each row has the colour (click the coloured square), how much wider the layer is than the letters, its height and 「穴なし」, which fills the holes in letters such as O and A. 「角」 sets how a wider layer goes round the corners of the letters: 「丸」, 「ベベル」 or 「鋭角」. The top row is the letters themselves. + adds a layer at the bottom, – takes the bottom layer away. A tag has two to six layers. 「キーホルダー用の穴」: gives the bottom layer a straight tab with a round end and a hole for a key ring; the tab grows with the hole. A 3 mm hole, the default, makes a tab 6.5 mm wide that sticks out 6.75 mm, the hole's edge 2 mm from the edge of the bottom layer. Choose the 「穴の直径」 and the 「側」: 「左」, 「右」 or 「上」. 「自由」 takes the hole off the tag and puts a 「キーホルダー用のタブ」 of its own beside it, in the bottom layer's colour and height: an ordinary shape you move and turn with its handles wherever the tag needs it.
