The ribbon cables can come out as well: 「フラットケーブルをふたの上へ」 opens the camera, display and PCIe connectors up through a lid, 「フラットケーブルを壁の横へ」 lays an opening from each across its long side - the way the cable leaves it - to the nearer edge and on by the reach; on the Raspberry Pi 5 the camera and display cables come out at the PCIe end, the three openings one above the other, on the Pi 4 and 3 B+ the camera's above the display's. 「GPIOヘッダーをふたの上へ」 takes the pin header up through the lid, for a HAT or jumper wires. What goes up reaches 「上への延長」 over its top, at least 20 mm, and gets the clearance round it.

A screw head often should not stand proud. The 「座ぐり」 cuts a round pocket for a socket-head screw (DIN 912), the 「皿穴」 a cone for a countersunk screw (DIN 7991). Both stand with the head end up: the 「頭部の直径」 is the diameter of the pocket or the cone, the 「軸の直径」 the bore below it, the 「全長」 the whole length. On the counterbore you set the 「頭部の深さ」, on the countersink the 「円錐の角度」 (90° suits countersunk screws). The defaults fit an M3 screw. The 「両側皿穴」 is a hole chamfered on both faces, for a plate that is to look neat on its front and its back. It has no entry of its own in the shape library: take the 「皿穴」 and switch on 「両側」 in its properties (bodies that are a double countersink already show the switch on): a cone at each end opens to the 「頭部の直径」, with the 「軸の直径」 between them. You set the 「円錐の角度」 and the 「全長」 as before. If the hole is too short for two full cones, they meet in the middle at that angle and the shaft stays wider than you set: a head of 10 mm, a shaft of 6 mm, 90° and a length of 2 mm make two cones from 10 down to 8 mm. As a hole it is pushed through a part like the others. Make the shape a hole and group it with the part. Let its top end a little above the surface the head should sit on, so the pocket opens cleanly. For the pocket of a hex nut, use a 「多角形」 with six sides as a hole. Under 「ねじサイズ」 you pick M2 to M30 (the countersink up to M20), and the shaft (clearance hole to ISO 273, medium), head diameter and depth or angle follow the standard (DIN 974-1, ISO 15065); the length stays. On the hexagon, 「ナット用くぼみ」 sets the width across flats and the height of an ISO 4032 nut, with 0.4 mm of room for printing. A drilled blind hole does not end flat but in the cone of the drill's tip (Discussion #621). The 「座ぐり」, the 「皿穴」 and a 「円柱」 set as a hole can end that way: under 「Bottom」, pick a drill point of 90°, 118° (a common twist drill) or 135°, or 「Drill point, other angle」 and type the angle under 「Point angle」, from 60° to 150°. As in a drawing, the depth – the cylinder's 「高さ」, the screw hole's 「全長」 – counts to the shoulder where the cone begins; the tip lies beyond it, about 0.3 times the diameter at 118°, and the line under the angle says how far. The cone is as wide as the hole, on a screw hole as wide as its shaft. 「Flat」 leaves the bottom as it always was. A solid cylinder keeps its flat end, and so does the double countersink, which goes through. A slotted hole leaves a part room to be moved a little before the screw is tightened, to line it up (Discussion #1531). Switch on 「長穴」 on the 「座ぐり」, the 「皿穴」 or the 「両側皿穴」: the pocket or the cone and the shaft then run round the two ends of a slot and straight along its sides. 「長穴の長さ」 sets how far; it starts as long as the head is wide and runs along the width, so turn the hole to point it another way. The 「頭部の直径」 and the 「ねじサイズ」 change the head and keep the slot. A slotted hole has no drill point, and like the round one it is an exact body. The 「化粧座金」 (a rosette, Discussion #1131) is the domed washer that goes under a countersunk or raised countersunk screw, for a tidy look on wood or a cover. It is a solid part, flat underneath; from a low rim a dome rises to the seat, a cone for the screw head, with the bore below it. Under 「ねじサイズ」 you pick M2 to M20: the bore is the clearance hole and the seat the countersink of that size, the 「直径」 and 「高さ」 follow from them (M3: 10.3 by 2.95 mm, M6: 16.6 by 4.5 mm). You can also set the 「直径」, 「高さ」, 「中心穴」, the 「頭部の直径」 at the top of the seat and its 「円錐の角度」 yourself. It stays round, and it is an exact body, so the edge tool and STEP work on it.

The 「Screw boss」 is the post a lid or a board is screwed to in an enclosure: a round post with a hole from the top. Under 「Fastener」 you choose what goes into it. A 「Heat-set insert」 is a brass insert pressed in with a soldering iron: 「Size」 offers M2 to M5 and #2-56 to 1/4-20, the hole as the common inserts want it (M3: 4.0 mm for an insert 5.7 mm long), a millimetre deeper than the insert so the plastic it pushes aside has room, and the post about twice the hole. A 「Self-tapping screw for plastics」 cuts its own thread: ST2.2 to ST4.2 (DIN 7981), plastics screws of 2.5 to 5 mm (K25–K50) or #2 to #10, with a pilot hole of about 0.8 times the screw, the post 2.5 times it and the hole 2.5 screws deep. 「Hole of my own」 takes the diameter and depth you type in. 「Hole diameter」, 「Hole depth」 and 「Outer diameter」 can be changed by hand; below the diameter the panel says how thick the wall round the hole is, and warns when it is thinner than the fastener wants. A hole as deep as the post goes through. The hole's mouth has a small chamfer, so the insert or the screw finds its way in. 「Gussets」 adds two to six thin ribs from the post down to the floor; 「Width with gussets」, 「Gusset height」 and 「Gusset thickness」 set how far out, how high and how thick they are. Stand the boss on the floor of a hollowed box and group it with the box; in the lid, a 「座ぐり」 as a hole over it takes the screw head. Set as a hole and grouped with a solid part, the boss cuts only its hole – the pocket for the insert or the screw, with its chamfer – so a block or a post of your own gets a blind hole for an insert; the hole opens where the boss's top is. Printed holes come out a little smaller than drawn: print one boss first and adjust 「Hole diameter」 by a tenth or two.

A lid that clicks shut needs no screws. The 「Snap-fit」 is a hook on a foot with its counterpart, the catch. With 「Part」 set to 「Hook and catch」 the two stand where they sit when snapped in, so you place them on lid and box together; 「Hook only」 or 「Catch only」 makes one of them. The barb has a slope below it that lets it slide in, the 「Entry angle」 (30° goes in easily), and above it the face that holds: at a 「Holding angle」 of 90° it holds for good, at 45° it can be pulled apart again. The 「Undercut」 is how far the barb reaches under the catch, 「Clearance」 the play between the two. The arm bends by the undercut as it goes in. Below 「Arm thickness」 the panel says how much it stretches at its root: PLA starts to break above about 2 %, PETG and ABS take about 4 %. A longer or thinner arm, or a smaller undercut, stretches less. The pair stands as it sits in a box printed upright, the lid on top: the hook hangs from its foot, the catch's top slopes at 45°, and only its holding face, as wide as the undercut, reaches out flat, so it prints on the wall without support. Put the pair where the lid meets the box wall: the hook's foot under the lid, the catch's back against the inside of the wall. 「パーツを分離」 then splits them into two bodies; group the hook with the lid and the catch with the box. If you can, print the lid so the arm lies flat: an arm standing up bends across its layers and breaks more easily.

The 「Rib」 stiffens a floor or a wall. As a 「Straight rib」 it is as long, high and thick as you set, its 「Top」 flat, round or chamfered. As a 「Gusset」 it is a triangle that braces a wall against the floor: 「Along the floor」 along the floor, 「Up the wall」 up the wall, both ends cut off short so they print cleanly. With 「Foot」 switched on, the rib stands on a thin plate along its whole length, centred under it and wider than it (a gusset's lies under its side along the floor), which holds it on the bed or the floor, so a thinner rib still stands. The foot starts three times as wide as the rib and 0.8 mm thick; 「Foot width」 is measured all the way across, so the shape is as wide as the foot, and 「Foot thickness」 from the bottom up. Under 「Foot shape」 the foot is 「Square」 or 「Oval」. The oval foot is an ellipse seen from above, without corners that could lift off the bed as the plastic shrinks while it cools. It is as wide as the foot and just long enough that at the rib's two ends it is still twice as wide as the rib, so the ends stand on it as well (under a gusset it is half an ellipse, from the wall to past the tip). On a foot narrower than about 2.7 times the rib the ellipse would get long: it stops at one and a half times the rib's length, but never so short that the ends stand on nothing. The shape grows by what reaches past the ends; the rib keeps its length. A rib about as thick as the wall or a little thinner, a multiple of the line width (0.8 or 1.6 mm with a 0.4 mm nozzle), and a few times as high as it is thick stiffens without pulling the wall out of shape. Several in a row come from 「パターン」; group them with the box.

Tape measure, ruler and framing square, distances to the origin, notes that stay attached to a part, and reference points that things snap to. To build a part exactly, you need to measure. layerling has several tools for that. None of them ends up in an export. Wall thickness and gaps inside a part are best measured in the section view with 「計測」.

The tape measure sits at the lower end of the view bar on the left edge (「メジャー」). It measures distances between corners, edges and faces. A click on it opens five buttons. If they cover what you want to measure, drag them by the grip on the left anywhere on the workplane; a double-click on the grip puts them back: The tape measure with its buttons: add measurement, move measuring points, remove measurement, whole edges, delete all measurements. 「寸法を追加」: Click one point, drag to the next and click it. The distance is labelled, with the axes it runs along in front: X, Y or Z for a straight one, XY, XZ or YZ across a plane, 3D for all three. Hover over the label to see how far it reaches along each axis, over a point to see its coordinates. While you place the second point, the axes, the distance and the reach along each axis show beside the pointer. A measurement that lies mostly behind another body fades; hovering its line or label brings it back. On an opposing edge or face, the second point snaps in at a right angle to the first when the pointer comes near - or anywhere on that edge or face while you hold Shift. Along the same face or on the workplane, Shift keeps the measurement straight along the main axis. Besides corners and edges, a point snaps to the middle of the flat face under the pointer and to the centre of a round edge, such as the rim of a hole or of a cylinder: a small cross in a circle marks the centre on offer, and when the pointer comes near, the point snaps in and a hint says what it is the centre of (「Centre of face」, 「Centre of hole」 or 「Centre of circle」). 「寸法の点を移動」: Grab the points and move them, the number follows. 「寸法の一部を削除」: Afterwards click a measurement to remove it. While 「寸法を追加」 is active, holding Shift or Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) and clicking a measurement point or line deletes it right away without switching modes. 「エッジ全体を計測」: A click on an edge measures all of it. A round edge says its diameter (Ø), the rim of a hole or of a cylinder for example, and an arc its radius (R); point at the number to see the length along the edge. With this switched off, a click puts a point on the edge instead, and the second point goes anywhere, so you can measure the diameter or any other distance. Alt turns the switch round for one click. On a circle, the point across from the first one snaps in when the pointer comes near, and the points sit on the true circle, so the diameter comes out exact. 「すべての寸法を削除」: Removes every measurement at once. Because this cannot be undone, layerling asks first; with no measurements there is nothing to do. 「真ん中を基準点にする」: In the middle of every measurement sits a small round mark, its lower half filled. It puts a reference point in the middle of the measurement: after a click on a round edge, such as the rim of a hole, in the centre of that circle - on an imported mesh too, where nothing else marks the middle of a hole - and for a diameter or any straight measurement halfway along it. A shape you drag then snaps to the point with its centre. A point that is there already is not made twice. The tape measure snaps to a reference point like to a corner, so you can measure from the centre of a circle or from the middle of a line: mark it, then click the point. 「長さを入力:2点目の形状が線に沿って移動します。負の長さでは1点目を越えて移動します」: When at least one end of a straight measurement sits on a body, its number can be clicked. Type a new length and press Enter: the body at the second point moves along the measured line until the distance is exactly that, as with the ruler in Tinkercad. If only the body at the first point is selected, that one moves instead. The measuring points stay on the body, so the measurement follows. Measure from a corner, an edge or the centre of a face or a hole to place parts at an exact distance: from the centre of a hole to the middle of a cylinder's top, the cylinder moves centre to centre. A negative length takes it that far past the first point, say 5 mm inside the edge of a box. A reference point belongs to no body, so between two of them nothing moves. When the measurement runs along two or three axes, the field also has a box under the length for each of them (ΔX, ΔY, ΔZ, the reach shown when you point at the number): type there instead, and the body moves along that axis only. Tab goes from box to box, Esc closes the field without moving anything. Pointing at the number tells which body will move, or why none can: it is locked, both points lie on the same body, or neither lies on a body. The message afterwards says what moved and how far; one undo takes it back. Esc leaves measuring mode.

You fetch the 「定規」 from the shape library. It is purely a measuring tool: it appears in no export and can neither be grouped nor cut. For every body that touches or overlaps the ruler, it shows the extent as a floating number right in the view. You can change that number right there, and the body follows. Stand the ruler up or tip it, and it measures along its own direction: upright beside a body it shows the body's height. The floating plus symbol creates a copy of the measured shape; it is there while the ruler lies flat. Its printed scale is in millimetres along one long edge, with the tens numbered, and in inches along the other, with a line every sixteenth of an inch and the whole inches numbered. The scale of the unit you work in (the switch at the bottom right) runs along the top edge; a ruler narrower than 15 mm carries only that one.

Sometimes you measure better at a right angle. Click 「角定規を配置」 in the view bar and then the workplane. A framing square with two arms at a right angle, with tick marks like a try square, is placed there. It has no body of its own either. Click close to the corner of a body, and its corner snaps exactly there. The design keeps the square where you set it, also in a saved .lyl file: when you open the design again, it is in the same place, turned the same way and measuring from the same points, until you remove it. If you need it in almost every design, switch on 「新しいデザインを原点に角定規を置いて開始」 under 「計測」 in the settings: every new design then starts with a framing square at the origin. The framing square lies on the workplane. If that sits on the side of a body, the square lies on that side too, see View and workplane. That is how you dimension on a vertical wall: put the workplane on the wall, place the square at its top left corner and click the handle until the arms point right and down. Dragging the handle moves it. A short click on the handle turns it by 90°. The × beside it removes it. Dragging the small circle at the end of an arm makes that arm longer or shorter, in whole millimetres. The lowest button under the handle, 「アームをビルドプレートと同じ長さに（アームの端をドラッグすると長さを変えられます）」, makes both arms as long as the build plate is wide and deep, for the printer set in the settings. The square keeps its arms' lengths with the design, and a square set again takes them over. The small button left of the handle switches what is measured from: the outside of a body (endpoint, an icon with lines) or its middle (midpoint, a crosshair). A small switch of the same kind sits beside each green number and sets that number alone: for a standing cylinder the middle in the two arms and the bottom in height, for a lying one the middle across and an end along. When all three agree again, the button at the handle shows the common mode. If bodies stand at one of the arms, the framing square shows their dimensions automatically, selected or not: bodies inside the square, beside an arm or across it. A body outside it, behind the corner or beside an arm from the outside, gets none. That works on the base plate only, not on the side of a body. The button with the arrow under the square's handle switches that off, so that only the selected bodies show their dimensions; it is kept with the design. When you select a body, the framing square shows in green how far it is from the corner, along both arms and in height. Click a green number to type a distance, and the body moves exactly there. With several bodies selected, they count as one: the ruler measures their shared outline, and a typed value moves them all together without changing their positions relative to each other. The guide lines of the green numbers run along the floor, the plane the framing square lies in, to the point below or beside the body; the height has its own arrow. The switch of each number sits in the frame of the number. The arms and the ticks are lines in the room: a body in front of them hides them, as a real square would be hidden. The small eye below the handle switches that: with the eye struck through, bodies hide the square (the start); with the eye open, the square stays in view over everything. The numbers on the arms fade where a body stands in front of them. With the midpoint, the green numbers count to the middle of the body, in height as well. That way you place a sphere with its centre exactly 15 mm from an edge, without subtracting the radius. On a wall you place a hole 40 mm from the left and 190 mm from the top like this: select the hole, switch to midpoint, type 40 and 190. The height there counts outward from the wall. Both the tape measure and the framing square stay where they are while you sketch and come back to the 3D view. Neither is in the history. The framing square is kept with the design, and so are the measurements of the tape measure, in the browser and in the .lyl file: they are there again when you open the design. The eye button among the tape measure's buttons hides all measurements and shows them again; whether they are hidden is kept as well, and adding, moving or deleting a measurement shows them first.

Click 「Protractor」 in the view bar to measure an angle. A row of buttons opens beside it, and until you click the button again or press Esc, a click in the view measures with the protractor. Like the tape measure, it snaps to the corners and edges of bodies; beside the bodies it sets a point on the plate. 「Angle from three points」: click the corner of the angle first, then a point on each side. While you place the last point, the angle shows already; after the third click it stays, with an arc between the sides. It is the angle at the corner, from 0° to 180°. 「Angle between two faces」: click two flat faces. A short blue line on each shows which way it faces, and the label gives both angles the faces make, the smaller first: a 45° chamfer against the top reads 45° · 135°, two sides of a box just 90°. A curved face has no single direction, so the protractor asks for a flat one. The next click after a finished angle starts a new one, and 「Remove the angle」 removes it. The angle follows the bodies when they move or turn. Nothing of it is saved or goes into the history: it is gone when you put the protractor away.

h: Distances to the origin and while moving
t: In the settings under 「外観」 there are two switches for live dimensions: 「移動時の寸法を表示」 shows by how much you move while dragging. That includes lifting with the black arrow above a body; the way up or down shows at its front corner. The arrow keys show their way as well: the presses add up until you select something else or drag, and Ctrl+↑ and Ctrl+↓ show the way up or down. Once you let go, click such a number and type the exact distance; a minus goes down. 「原点からの距離を表示」 shows the distances of the selection to the origin of the plate, also with several selected bodies. With 「寸法を常に表示」 the dimensions stay visible permanently. A body that does not stand on the workplane also shows its height above it; click the number to type a new one. With 「Dimension boxes in axis colours」 each box takes the colour of its axis, as the handles do: red for X, green for Y and blue for Z. So on a small part you see at a glance which number is which. For a moment without them, press Q: the sizes and distances around the selection disappear, so a part you move is easy to see. Q again brings them back. A handle you point at still shows its size.

Parts that should move after printing - a flexi dragon, a hinge printed in place, a box and its lid, an axle in its bore - need a gap between them. Too little, and they stick together; overlapping, they print as one piece. 「Check clearance」, next to 「スケッチ間のロフト」, checks that before you print. It takes the selected objects, or every visible object when nothing is selected (the same ones an export takes), and checks each pair: 「Overlap」 (red): the two share a volume. It shows red inside the bodies, which turn see-through, and the list says how large it is. 「Touching」 (red): they touch and fuse when printed. 「Too tight」 (orange): the narrowest gap is smaller than 「Minimum gap」. 「Fine」 (green): the narrowest gap is at least that wide. Each row names the two parts and, for a gap, its width and where it lies: 「side by side」 (within one layer) or 「between layers」 (above or below: there the slicer can only leave whole layers free, so a gap thinner than one layer closes). Click a row: the camera goes there, both parts are outlined, and a line with the number marks the narrowest place. Pairs further apart than 5 mm are not listed. Nothing in the design changes: the check saves nothing and leaves nothing to undo. 「Minimum gap」 starts at 0.3 mm; 0.3 is tight, 0.4 usual for a print in place. Changing it sorts the list again at once, without a new check, and the browser keeps the value. 「Check the separate parts of one object (print in place)」 (on to start) checks the separate parts of one object against each other too: a flexi dragon or a hinge imported as one STL is one object, but its links are separate parts. They are listed as "Name · Part 2". A part inside a cavity of another, a ball in a cage, is a part of its own. If you change the design while the panel is open, it shows 「Changed – check again」; click that or 「Check again」. Esc or 「Close」 closes the panel. Scaling changes the gaps too: a flexi model scaled to 70 % keeps 70 % of its gaps, so check again after scaling. The check measures the triangle mesh the slicer gets. A round axle and its bore are polygons with their corners on the circle, so a gap can come out a few hundredths smaller than the round numbers. A pair with too many triangles is listed as 「Not checked」. An AI runs the same check with layerling_check_clearance.

A note records what the geometry does not say: "This screw is 0.3 mm too tight", "print the lid yet", "dimension from Peter". Place one with 「メモ」 or the N key. If you place the note on a body, it travels with it. If you place it beside, it stays on the workplane (「作業平面上」). 「オブジェクトから切り離す」 releases an attached note from the body. 「For the AI」 turns a note into a request for an AI agent on the MCP bridge (see "AI with MCP"): the agent reads it with layerling_list_notes, does the work and answers in the same note, under your text. It can also put notes of its own on the model, to ask or report something at a spot. Ask the agent to watch your notes, and it waits for them with layerling_wait_for_notes: you then only work on the model, and every new request is picked up as soon as you tick the box, without going back to the agent's window. 「グループ化」 takes an attached note into the group; 「グループ解除」 hands it to the visible part under it, a group inside included. While a group is open with 「グループを編集」, its notes move with the part under them and go back to the group with 「完了」; cancelling puts them back as they were. If its body is deleted, or no visible body is under it any more, the note stays where it stood, on the workplane. Dragging the pin moves the note. A click on the pin folds the card away, only the small number stays; another click opens it again. A click into the text edits it. While you write, Enter keeps the text and Esc puts it back to how it was before you started; Shift+Enter starts a new line. In a sketch, 「メモ」 or N places a note too, anywhere on the sketch. All of a sketch's notes belong to its body: in the 3D view they sit on it, on the top of an extruded or swept body and on the drawn profile of a revolved one, and move with it. When you open the sketch again it shows the body's notes, including those placed in 3D. In the sketch, Undo takes back a note like a line, and 「キャンセル」 discards what you changed in the notes. Shift+N shows or hides the notes here too. Notes are saved in the design, appear in no export and can be shown or hidden with 「メモと点を表示」 (in 「表示オプション」, the arrow beside the eye icon) or with Shift+N.

A reference point is a bare mark in space, like a pencil mark or a layout point in a workshop: it belongs to no body, is never printed, and other things snap to it. Right-click a body and choose 「中心に印を付ける」, 「角に印を付ける」 or 「エッジの中点に印を付ける」: the points appear on the top face of the body (of the whole selection, if you selected several). 「この面の中心に印を付ける」 puts one in the middle of the flat face you right-clicked instead, on a side or an end, say. With a pivot set, 「回転の中心に印を付ける」 puts one exactly on it, so another part's centre snaps to the point the selection turns about. Drag a point to move it: it snaps to the corners, the middles of the edges and faces of bodies, to their real corners and to other points; hold Alt to let it go free. Or click it to see its coordinates and type new ones; they use the unit you set. Each card can be dragged away by its title if it covers something, on its own: the others stay where they are, and a double-click on the title puts it back. The card you touched last stands in front of the others. Delete all in a card, or Delete all reference points in the right-click menu (of a body, or of an empty spot of the 3D view), deletes every point at once. 「削除」 removes it. The tape measure can mark a point too: 「真ん中を基準点にする」, the half-filled mark in the middle of a measurement, puts one in its middle, in the centre of a round hole for example. And it measures from a point: the tape snaps to reference points like to corners. When you drag a shape, its edges and its centre snap to a point, like they snap to other shapes (「移動中に他のシェイプにスナップ」). The framing square snaps to points too. Points are saved in the design, appear in no export, and are shown or hidden together with the notes by 「メモと点を表示」 (Shift+N). An AI can mark, list and remove them with layerling_add_reference_points, layerling_list_reference_points and layerling_remove_reference_points.

A reference image is a picture to line parts up on: lay a photo of a circuit board on the floor of its case, and place the standoffs, holes and connector cut-outs right on it. It is a guide, not a body: it is never printed, never exported (STL, 3MF, OBJ, STEP, SVG), never part of a group, a bundle or a cut, and the print estimate leaves it out. Open 「読み込み」 and choose 「参照画像」, then a PNG, JPG, WebP, GIF or BMP picture. It lands on the workplane - on the plate, or on the face you set the workplane on - with its longer side 100 mm, half see-through. Move, turn and resize it with its handles like any shape. A body in front of it is picked first, so working on top of it does not grab the picture. 「透過(%)」 in its settings fades it from solid to barely there. 「校正」 gives it its true size, as in the sketch: click two points on the picture whose real distance you know - two mounting holes of the board, say - and type that distance in 「実際の距離(mm)」. The picture keeps its proportions and its middle. Lock it with the lock in the header of its settings, and it stays put: clicks then go through it to the plate. Pick it in the object list to unlock it. The picture is saved once in the design file, however often it is copied or undone. A large picture makes the file larger by as much; the message when you add it says how large it is. An AI adds, moves, calibrates, fades and locks one with layerling_reference_image. With trace it traces the picture into a sketch body standing on it, as the sketch's 「トレース」 does.
Choosing your own printer, being warned when something does not fit, and laying the part the right way.

Open the settings (the cogwheel in the title row, 「ワークスペース設定」) and switch to the area 「作業平面」. Under 「プリンター」 you pick your printer from a list of over 230 common models, including Bambu Lab, Prusa, Creality, Anycubic, Elegoo and many more. The workplane settings with a printer chosen. Print bed and maximum print height come from the slicer profile. Three things happen: The workplane takes the size of the print bed. In the corner of the workplane appear the printer's name and its build volume. If the writing gets in the way, switch it off with 「プレートのラベル」 under 「作業平面」; that also goes for the design's name at the front left. layerling warns when something does not fit. The printer profiles come from OrcaSlicer, so they are the same ones your slicer knows. If you would rather work without a printer, choose 「プリンターなし - 自由なサイズ」. You can also set the size of the workplane by hand. Delta printers such as those by FLSun or SeeMeCNC, or the Anycubic Predator, print on a round plate. With one of them the workplane is round too, as wide as the plate, and a body is too large as soon as it reaches past the rim. A round body is measured by its own outline, not by the box round it, so a cylinder nearly as wide as the plate still fits.

A body that sticks out over the edge of the print plate is marked. A message tells you which sides overhang and by how much. It is the same if the part is too tall: the height counts from the lowest body, just as the slicer sets the model down. The box is wider than the print bed of the Bambu Lab A1 mini. The message at the bottom says by how much. The warning does not stop you from working on. It is a hint so you do not find out only in the slicer that the part is too big. A part that is too big can often be split: cut it in two with 「分割」 and print both halves separately. If you park parts beside the plate on purpose, click the small cross in the message. The warning is then gone for exactly these bodies. Once one of them fits again and you move it out later, or another body sticks out, the message comes back. Hidden bodies never count, so hiding the parked parts works as well.

How a part lies on the plate decides its strength and looks. Two tools in the 「配置」 area help: 「面を下にして平らに置く」: click a face and the part lies with that side down. The best print direction in one click. 「作業平面に落とす」 (D): sets the part on the workplane when it floats somewhere in the air. A few rules of thumb for direction: Large flat faces down. They stick best. Lay long, loaded parts so the layers do not run perpendicular to the load. Layers are the weakest direction. Avoid overhangs steeper than 45°, or give them supports in the slicer.

In the menu next to the eye (「表示」), Show overhangs switches the overhangs on. Every face that points down more steeply than 45° is then hatched red and white - that is where the printer would need supports. What rests on the plate stays clear. So you see while designing whether a sphere, an arch or a horizontal hole prints without supports; the teardrop hole is made for exactly that. Turn the part or lay it on another face with 「面を下にして平らに置く」, and the hatching follows at once. How steep your printer manages is set in the settings under 「外観」: from 30° (careful) to 70° (for printers with good part cooling). A face resting on another body is still marked - layerling only looks at the face itself.

h: Support ribs for a tilted part
t: A part printed tilted on one edge, at 45° say, often needs no supports: its faces are steep enough. But it stands on a thin edge and can fall over. The 「サポートリブ」 holds it: a thin rib stands under its lower face a small gap away, on an oval foot, and tiny bridges hold the part to it. Turn the part onto its edge first and let it stand on the plate. Select the part and click 「サポートリブ」 in the 「変形」 group of the ribbon, right-click the part, or find it with Ctrl+K. Click the lower face where the rib should stand. The face must look down, slope between 15° and 75° and reach down to the plate; the rib stands straight down the face from your click. If the part's bottom edge is rounded or chamfered, the face may stop up to 3 mm above the plate: click the flat face above the rounding. Set 「ノズル」, 「積層ピッチ」 and 「最初の層」 as in your slicer. The rib is two lines of the nozzle thick, the gap to the part half a line; each bridge is one line wide and exactly one layer high and lies on a layer of the print, so the slicer prints it as one thin line that breaks off cleanly. 「リブの高さ」 is how high the rib reaches up the face (half way to start), 「ブリッジの間隔」 how far apart the bridges are, in whole layers. Under 「その他の設定」 the thickness, the gap, the bridges' width and the foot's thickness can be set by hand (until then they follow the nozzle and the layers), as can the foot's width and the roundings where the rib meets the foot and at its top. 「作成」 adds the rib. With 「パーツとまとめる」 (on to start) rib and part are bundled: they move together and go to the slicer as two bodies side by side, joined by the bridges in the print. The rib is a mesh body: to change it, delete it and make it again. Each click makes one rib; for more, click 「別の面」 or repeat it with 「パターン」. The rib must not run into the part anywhere, and the part must stand on the plate - otherwise the window says why. Your settings are kept in this browser for the next rib. 「Check clearance」 and 「Print check」 know the rib: that its bridges reach into the part, and that the rib and its bridges are thin and lie one layer high across the gap, is meant to be so and is not reported. A rib made with layerling 1.148.0 does not carry this mark yet; make it again and the checks leave it out.

Walls should be at least two extrusion lines wide, so 0.8 mm with a 0.4 mm nozzle. Sturdy parts need 1.2 to 2 mm. Where two parts fit into each other you need clearance: usually 0.2 to 0.4 mm, depending on the printer. Make a small test pair before you print the big part. Many people lightly chamfer the lower edge that sits on the plate. That keeps the first layer from spreading ("elephant foot").

h: Your printer's play: the fit test
t: Every printer prints holes a little smaller and pins a little thicker than they are drawn, each by its own amount, so the clearance two printed parts need is a guess at first. Measure it once instead. In the settings under 「作業平面」, 「Make fit test」 puts a fit test on the plate: a 60 × 20 × 4 mm plate with seven holes for one 5 mm pin, each drawn 5 mm plus twice 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30 or 0.40 mm, the value raised beside it, and the 5 mm pin itself, standing beside the plate with a small chamfer on top. It is made of ordinary shapes, so it prints with the rest of the plate, without supports. On a printer whose bed moves back and forth, the tall, thin pin can wobble loose or come out wavy at its foot, brim or not. Tick 「Test pin on a breakaway base」 before you make the fit test: the pin then stands on a small 10 mm plate that holds on to the bed. It does not touch the plate's socket but rests on a small nub in its floor; once printed, bend the pin to and fro and it snaps off. Print it as it lies, then push the pin, chamfered end first, into the holes from the tightest on. The snuggest hole the pin still turns in gives your printer's play. Type its number under 「Printer play」, or click it among the values below the field. The play is per side, in millimetres, and the browser keeps it for every design; an empty field means not measured. With several printers, choose the one you print on under 「プリンター」 first: each printer keeps a play of its own, and new uses start from the play of the printer the design is set to. A printer without one uses the play set while no printer was chosen. From then on, new uses start from the play instead of the built-in value: 「片側のすき間」 and 「Pin play (per side)」 in the 「ふた」 tool, the clearance of a new 「あり溝」 and 「Snap-fit」, 「クリアランス (XY)」 of a new nut or tapped hole - twice the play, as that is the room across the whole diameter - and 「Minimum gap」 in 「Check clearance」. The same goes for 「Clearance per side」 of the dowels, plugs and dovetails in 「分割」. While such a field still holds that value, "「From your fit test」" beside it says where the number comes from. A hinge printed in place and the joints of the 「フレキシジョイント」 tool keep their 0.4 mm: printed in one piece, their gaps also have to stay open between the layers, which a pin printed apart does not measure. Room for pressing in a magnet or a Gridfinity key, and room for a bought socket or board, keep their own values too. Bodies already in a design never change, nor does a design you open.

「Print check」, next to 「Check clearance」 in 「結合」, looks at the selected objects, or at every visible object when nothing is selected, and says in one window what would go wrong when printing. Each of its five lines is green when it found nothing, and orange with what and where when it did: 「Thin walls」: places thinner than two lines of the nozzle - 0.8 mm with a 0.4 mm nozzle. The slicer leaves such a wall out or prints it as one weak line. Choose your nozzle under 「Nozzle」 at the top of the window (0.2 to 0.8 with one click, any other in the field). The thin places are painted red with a light grid on the bodies, and the line names the thinnest place and how much surface is too thin. Places smaller than 1 mm² and sharp edges, such as the edge of a wedge, are left out. 「Floating parts」: a body, or a separate part of one, that touches neither the plate nor another part (within 0.05 mm). It would be printed in the air. A part resting on a part that stands is fine. 「Small contact with the plate」: a part on the plate whose first layer is very small for its height, such as a sphere or a cone on its tip. It can come loose while it prints. The check warns below 0.5 mm² of footprint, measured 0.1 mm above the plate, for each millimetre of height: a sphere is always below that, a cube of 10 mm has 10. 「Overhangs」: the same figures as Show overhangs, at the angle set there. 「Open mesh」: an imported mesh with open edges, or edges that three or more faces share. The slicer has to guess where such a mesh is inside. A tray whose right wall is only 0.6 mm thick: Print check paints it red and names it in the window. 「Show」 on a line takes the camera there; it selects the floating parts, those standing on too little and the open meshes, and for the overhangs it switches Show overhangs on. Bodies that overlap are checked joined, as the slicer joins them. If you change the design while the window is open, it shows 「Changed – check again」; click that or 「Check again」. Esc closes the window. Nothing in the design changes. An AI runs the same check with layerling_check_print.

Choose 「エクスポート」 and then STL or 3MF. STL is the simplest format. 3MF keeps names and colours of the individual bodies and is therefore handy when you print in several colours. The export window also shows how many grams and metres of filament the part would take printed solid. More in Files and saving.
Where your designs live, how to back them up, which formats layerling imports and exports, and what is possible on a shared server.

layerling saves everything in the browser on your computer. There is no account and nothing is uploaded. (With a copy you host yourself, designs can live in a shared folder on the server instead; see the section on the shared folder further down.) Every change saves itself. The preview picture on the start page shows the view you last had in front of you when you went back with 「ホームに戻る」. If you open layerling in the same browser days later, everything is there. If you go back to the start page from a design with nothing in it, layerling asks whether to keep it. 「はい」 or Enter keeps it, 「いいえ」 removes it, so empty designs do not pile up. For a design in a shared folder on a server, 「いいえ」 deletes the file from the server, for everyone who uses it. That has a downside: whoever clears the browser storage or switches to another computer loses the designs. So back up important work into a file.

With dozens of designs a single list is not enough. On the start page, 「新しいフォルダー」 makes a folder for the designs of this browser; a click on the folder opens it. Folders can hold folders. Into a folder: drag a design onto the folder, or choose 「移動先 …」 in the design's menu, which lists every folder. A new design, and a file you open or import, made while a folder is open lands in that folder. Out again: the first tile in a folder, .., and the line under the tabs lead back; you can drop a design on them too. A folder dragged onto another folder goes inside it. Rename and delete are in the folder's menu. Deleting a folder deletes no design: what was in it moves one level up. Search looks through every folder; a design that is found shows its folder, and a click on it opens the folder. 「すべてバックアップ」 keeps the folders: the designs sit in the backup file in their folders, and restoring the backup puts them back there. The folders of this browser are separate from the folders on a server. The card pictures go into the file too, so they are back as soon as you restore.

On the start page every design has a menu with the options to rename, duplicate and delete. The row beside the tabs has the same buttons on every tab. To delete several designs at once, click 「選ぶ」: a click on a card chooses it (a tick shows what is chosen), 「すべて選ぶ」 chooses every design in the list, and 「削除」 asks once for all of them. 「完了」 or Esc leaves the selection. With 「すべてバックアップ」 you pack all designs of the open tab into one single ZIP file. 「バックアップを戻す」, beside it (it is there on a new computer with no designs, too), brings them back, also in another browser or on another computer; 「デザインを開く、またはジオメトリを読み込む」 takes the same file. The 「カスタムシェイプ」 travel in the same file, in the folder Custom shapes, see Shapes. If you restore a backup into a browser that already has some of these designs, those are not added a second time; the notice says how many were already there. A design that cannot be read is left out, and the notice names it. If the page reloads in the middle of a backup, usually because a very large design took all the memory the browser allows, the start page says afterwards at which design it stopped: save that one on its own as a file (see below) or simplify its largest meshes, then back up again. Above the designs of this browser, a short line reminds you that they are kept nowhere else. Only some designs: after 「選ぶ」, 「バックアップ」 packs just the chosen designs, in their folders, into one ZIP file, and 「バックアップ」 in a folder's menu packs that folder with every design and folder in it. Neither takes the custom shapes along, and 「バックアップを戻す」 brings both back like a full backup. This is for the designs of this browser. Where a backup goes: in Chrome and Edge a save dialog asks for the folder and the name, and it remembers the folder for the next backup. That way your backups go straight into a folder of your own, on a cloud drive for example. The same goes for 「カスタムシェイプをバックアップ」. Other browsers put the file into their download folder; which folder that is, you set in the browser's settings. If a design opens very slowly or not at all, usually because its history of undo steps has grown very large, choose 「Open without history」 in its menu on the start page. layerling then reads only the current state, deletes every earlier step for good and opens the design; after a question, because this cannot be undone. To keep the steps, back the design up with 「バックアップ」 first. You back up a single design in the editor: 「エクスポート」, choose the format LYL and click 「layerlingデザインを保存」. The LYL file is layerling's own design format and contains everything: shapes, groups, sketches, CAD data, imported sources and the history, meaning the undo steps. Under 「保存する操作履歴」 you choose how many of the last steps travel along; it starts at what the settings (the cogwheel in the ribbon) keep under 「履歴」. The last stop, 「なし」, saves the design with its current state only - the way to share a file without its undo steps. The export is a copy under the 「ファイル名」 you give it; the design in your browser keeps its history. Older .skf files from earlier versions can still be opened; they are then saved as .lyl. Saving into your own folder (Chrome and Edge). There the button opens your system's save dialog, so you pick the folder and the name yourself, and an existing file can be replaced. Afterwards Ctrl+S saves the design into that same file again, without a dialog. A design opened from a .lyl file with 「デザインを開く、またはジオメトリを読み込む」 or the open button of the export window saves back into that file, too. The browser may ask once for permission to change the file. After the page is reloaded the design forgets its file, and the next Ctrl+S asks for it again; the dialog starts in the folder you used last. Firefox and Safari do not allow a page to write into files like this. There the file is downloaded to the Downloads folder as before, and Ctrl+S downloads it again; Firefox can be set to ask for the folder each time under Settings, General, Downloads. If you give the file a different name there, the design keeps its own name, since a version or a date in the file name is often meant that way; the message after saving then offers 「デザインもこの名前にする」. When the save dialog saves nothing. If the dialog closes without a file, the message at the top says so and offers 「Download instead」: the design then goes to the Downloads folder like in Firefox. The browser reports a dialog closed with Cancel the same way as one it could not use, so on a PC where the save dialog fails for every folder this is the way to keep saving.

Instructions, a parts list, notes, a photo or a datasheet can stay with the design as files. 「添付ファイル」 in the 「ファイル」 group of the ribbon, the paperclip, opens the list; a small dot on the paperclip shows that the design has some. 「ファイルを添付」: Choose one or more files: .md (Markdown) or .txt as plain text (UTF-8), .png, .jpg, .jpeg or .webp pictures, or .pdf documents. A file is checked by its content, so a file that is not what its name says is refused, and other types, .svg among them, cannot be attached. A text file can be at most 2 MB, a picture 16 MB and a PDF 32 MB; a design holds up to 32 files and 64 MB together. The list: The arrow downloads a file as it was uploaded. The bin removes it; the row asks once more first, and a removed file cannot be brought back with undo, because attachments are not part of the undo history. Reading a file: The eye on the row of a .md or .txt file opens it in a window to read, without downloading it. Markdown is shown formatted, with headings, lists, tick boxes, tables and code; a text file is shown exactly as it is written. Only links to web pages and e-mail addresses work, and they open in a new tab. Pictures named in the file are not loaded: their description stands in their place. Escape, the cross or a click beside the window closes it. Reading works in the History view too. Looking at a picture: The eye on the row of a picture opens it in the same window, shrunk to fit when it is large. A PDF has no eye: download it and open it in the program you read PDF files with. A name that is already there: layerling asks what to do. 「置きかえる」 puts the new content into the file of that name, which keeps its place in the list. 「名前を変更」 adds the new file under another name and suggests the first free one, such as notes 2.md. The cross leaves the new file out. Upper and lower case count the same, and the same file uploaded again changes nothing. Attachments are saved with the design like everything else: in the browser, in a LYL file, in a backup and in a design on a server, which they reach as soon as one is added or removed. They do not come along with 「このデザインに挿入」 or with a custom shape, and a bug report does not contain them. A design with attachments is saved as a newer kind of LYL file: an older layerling says that it cannot open it instead of dropping the files. A design without attachments is saved exactly as before.

Click 「エクスポート」 or press Ctrl+E. If the window covers something, drag it by its title bar to another spot; the Import and Attachments windows move the same way. A double click on the title bar puts it back. The export window with the formats STL, 3MF, OBJ, STEP, SVG, PNG, LYL and 2D. At the top is the file name, below it you choose the format. With something selected, only the selection is exported, otherwise the whole design. If the selection leaves out visible parts, a note in the window says so plainly, and 「すべて選択」 selects everything visible in one click. Once the file is written, the window closes by itself; if the export fails, it stays open with the message. Format For What to know STL slicer and 3D printing A triangle mesh. The simplest and most widespread format. An STL has no parts: bodies that overlap are joined into one mesh. To keep them as separate parts, export 3MF. In Chrome and Edge the first STL export asks where to save, and later STL exports of the design write into that file, until you type another name in the file name field or press 「名前を付けて保存…」. 3MF slicer with colours Every body stays a part of its own with name and colour. Overlapping bodies are only joined when they share a colour; where a shape sits inside one of another colour, say a logo in a plate, the one built first leaves room for the later one. Suited to PrusaSlicer, Bambu Studio, OrcaSlicer and Cura. Bambu Studio and OrcaSlicer ask on opening how to map the colours onto your filaments, and call the file "not from Bambu" - the message is harmless. OrcaSlicer and the slicers built on it do not read a colour per face, though. A file with a body of several colours, such as a Gridfinity bin with letters in a colour of their own or a group with 「マルチカラー」 on, therefore also has every face painted with its colour's filament, as painting in the slicer would: OrcaSlicer and PrusaSlicer 2.9 then print each colour with its filament, PrusaSlicer up to 15 colours, and Bambu Studio 2.9 takes the filaments from the painting instead of asking. OBJ modelling and exchange A widely supported mesh format. Colours are stored as vertex colours in the same file, with no extra .mtl. Bambu Studio and OrcaSlicer read them and ask, as with 3MF, how to map them onto your filaments; other programs see only the shape. As with 3MF, overlapping bodies are only joined when they share a colour. STEP a full CAD program Keeps boxes, cylinders, spheres and cones as exact geometry, and so shapes made from an outline (star, heart, ellipse, tube, half sphere, round roof, rounded box, dovetail, the bores and more), the bent tube, the wedge, the pyramid, the paraboloid, the curved cone, threads, springs and gears, plus fillets and chamfers. The first STEP export in a session loads the CAD kernel (about 22 MB) once. SVG laser cutter and plotter A clean top view in millimetres, including holes and curved outlines. Under 「表示」, 「作業面への接地面」 writes only the outlines where the objects stand on the workplane. 「上から見える辺」 writes the edges you see from above as lines, each body in its colour; see below. DXF laser cutting shop The same top view (「上から見たシルエット」 or 「作業面への接地面」) as one outline of lines, true arcs and circles - no polylines, splines or curves made of short straight pieces - on layer 0 in white, DXF 2000 in millimetres, not mirrored. Bodies that touch become one outline, so no line is cut twice. Shops ask for one part per file: select the part before exporting. Not yet tried on a laser cutter: feedback is welcome. PNG forum posts, print sites, questions A picture of the view as it is, at twice the resolution and without handles, selection frames and dimensions. 「プリントベッドを表示」 and 「背景を透明にする」 are chosen in the window. Turn and zoom first until the picture is right; the selection does not matter here. LYL layerling itself The editable design with everything that belongs to it. 2D workshop, lathe and mill, documentation A drawing at 1:1 as PDF or SVG: front, top and right-side views on an ISO sheet. See below. Bridges for parts that would fall out (DXF and SVG). When a plate with text is cut by a laser or a plotter, the middle of letters like o, a and b falls out. Tick 「落ちてしまうパーツにブリッジを付ける」 in the export window of the DXF, or of the SVG with the top view, and small bridges hold such parts to the material round them, as on a stencil: 「ブリッジの幅」 (0.5 to 3 mm) and 「パーツごとのブリッジの数」 (1 to 4) are set beside it. A bridge never touches another outline or another bridge and never leaves a gap too narrow to cut; parts that would only hold each other are tied to the plate too. If a part gets no bridge at the chosen width, the message after the export says how many. Nothing changes unless the box is ticked. STL into your own folder (Chrome and Edge). There the first STL export of a design opens your system's save dialog, so you pick the folder and the name yourself and can replace an existing file. After that every STL export of the design writes into that same file without a dialog; the export window shows which file, and Save as… next to the export button picks another. The dialog remembers its own folder, apart from the one for designs, so the slicer files can stay with the slicer. After the page is reloaded the design forgets its STL file and the next export asks again. Firefox and Safari download the file as before. If you would rather have every STL as a plain download, so that the browser numbers a name it has already used (name (1).stl, name (2).stl) as Tinkercad does, switch on 「STLを上書きせずにダウンロードする」 in the settings under 「外観」. A hole you have not grouped is taken out of every body it reaches when you export, as the view shows it. So there is no need to group before each export. With a selection, only the selected holes count. A hole cannot be exported on its own; layerling points that out. STEP only carries exact CAD bodies. An imported mesh is made exact for the file, as 「Make exact」 does (see "Making an imported mesh exact" below), which can make the export take up to a minute; a mesh that is mostly free-form, such as a figure, is left out, as is anything else that cannot be written exactly. The message after the export names those bodies and says why. For the printer, use STL or 3MF, which carry everything.

h: SVG for a laser or plotter
t: With 「上から見える辺」 under 「表示」, the SVG shows the design as you see it from above, like the top view of a drawing: every edge you can see is a line, and edges hidden by other parts are left out. Each line has the colour of its body, so a laser or plotter program that sorts by colour puts each colour on a layer of its own. Whether a layer is cut, scored or engraved, you choose there. Every area a colour shows has a closed outline, and where two bodies meet, both get the line. The areas are filled even-odd, so filling a colour to engrave it leaves its holes and the places of other bodies free. A part reaching through another gets the line where it comes out. The SVG is at 1:1 in millimetres, with the front of the design at the bottom of the page, in the same place as the silhouette. A design with too many edges for this view, such as a plate with hundreds of holes, gets its filled silhouette instead, and the message after the export says so.

Choose the format 2D (hover over it and it says Drawing) and, below the file name, PDF or SVG. With something selected, only the selection is drawn, otherwise the whole visible design; holes you have not grouped still cut the parts they reach. layerling draws the front, top and right-side views in first-angle layout (the right side to the left of the front view, the top view below it) on the smallest ISO sheet that fits, from A4 to A0, or a larger one if the part needs it. It is always at 1:1. Each view carries its overall width and height, and edges you cannot see are dashed. Round bores that run parallel to a view direction get a centre cross and a label (F1, T1, R1), and a table at the bottom lists their diameter and position, measured from the lower-left corner of the view. The title block in the lower-right corner holds the name, scale, units, date and sheet number. The words on the sheet follow the interface language. Print at 100 % or "actual size", or the lengths will not match. What the drawing does not do: threads, depths, tolerances and bores at an angle are not dimensioned, and the sizes come from the model as a mesh, so they are nominal. A very detailed part (over 100,000 triangles) or more than 200 bores is refused with a message; choose fewer objects then. The projection is based on the drawing work of Cadverix-3D by WC3D.

h: How much filament does it take?
t: For STL, 3MF, OBJ and STEP the 「材料」 box shows the volume, weight and length of 1.75 mm filament of what is exported. It counts like the file: visible bodies only, holes taken off, overlaps only once. On the right you pick the filament - PLA, PETG, ABS, ASA, TPU or PA (nylon) - and the weight follows its density. The volume is the body's own. Weight and filament are a rough estimate for a print with walls and infill: you set the 「インフィル」 (15 % to begin with) and the 「壁」 (2) under the heading, and the box says what it counted and what the same part would weigh solid. Your slicer's own settings decide the real number, so take it as a guide: good for comparing designs and for whether the spool will last. At 100 % infill the box counts the part as solid, the upper bound. The box works out its numbers when you press 「計算する」, so the export window opens at once even for a finely traced model.

With 「読み込み」 or Ctrl+I you bring foreign files into the design. The import window: open or insert designs and drop geometry. 「layerlingデザインを開く」: A layerling design (.lyl, or an older .skf) comes back as a new design. 「このデザインに挿入」: The bodies of a layerling design are added to the open one. Handy for basic shapes you need again and again: build them once, save them and bring them in every time. Drop one or more .lyl files on the drop zone below and they are inserted the same way. Its notes come along, closed and numbered on after the ones already in the design, and so do its reference points. 「Insert from the server」: The same for a design kept on the server (shown when there is a server store). Pick the folder and click the design; its bodies are added to the open one. DXF: A DXF, as a laser cutting shop or a supplier sends a part outline, comes in as parts to work on: every closed outline a body 4 mm high and every hole in it a hole of its own beside it (a round one a cylinder), so a hole is moved and sized in the 3D editor like any other; select them all to move the part. In millimetres (a file in inches is converted, one without a unit is read as millimetres), arcs and circles kept as true arcs. Lines, arcs, circles, ellipses, polylines, splines and blocks are read; text, dimensions and hatches are left out, and outlines that do not close too - the message says how many. Set the thickness in the properties. Add geometry: Drop STL, OBJ, 3MF, STEP, SVG, PNG or JPG files in the window or click to choose a file. Imported meshes can be turned, moved, cut with holes and built upon. A STEP file with several solids, an assembly from another CAD program, comes in as one body each under the name the file gives it, in its place to the others and in the colour the file gives it; several bodies under one entry of the file, the screws of a part say, become a part each. Its assemblies become bundles under their names, an assembly inside one a bundle inside the bundle; so a whole assembly hides or moves at once, and a double click opens it to work on a single part. An SVG comes in as a sketch body, one from a tracer such as picsvg.com or Inkscape's "Trace Bitmap" as well: its outlines become the lines and curves of a sketch, 4 mm high and reading from above as in the drawing. In the properties you set its 「塗り」, an area or a stroke outside, inside or centred, and 「シルエット（穴なし）」 leaves the holes out, see Sketches, "Fill and silhouette". You change the points themselves in sketch mode. If it should come in at a size of your own, type the width in the import window under SVG and picture: width in mm first, as in Tinkercad: the drawing is scaled to it, height and depth with it, and the field is empty again after that one import; left empty, an SVG comes in at its own size and a picture 50 mm wide. Only a very intricate SVG with more than 2500 lines and curves comes in as a fixed mesh. A PNG or JPG picture is traced into an outline and comes in the same way, as a sketch body 50 mm wide that you can resize afterwards: the part of the picture that is not its background, the background being the part that takes up more of the picture's edge. An SVG that holds nothing but one picture is traced the same way. A shape that cannot be built into a solid, such as an outline that crosses itself or touches itself at a point, is left out, and after the import layerling says how many there were. Then it helps to join overlapping pieces in the drawing program, close the outlines and save the file again. Drawings made on one page, such as the layers of one document exported as separate files, line up again when you switch on 「SVG: 図面ページ上の位置を保つ」 in the import window before you import them: each keeps its place on the page, where otherwise each is centred on itself. An SVG drawn in several colours comes in as one body per colour as well, each in its colour and in its place; with more than 12 colours, as a traced picture has, it stays one body. A coloured OBJ or 3MF comes in as one body per colour, each in its place. In an OBJ the colours sit either in the file itself, as in an OBJ from layerling, or in an .mtl beside it. Select that one too, or import the whole ZIP the way Tinkercad hands out its OBJ. A 3MF carries its colours itself, and in a project from Bambu Studio, OrcaSlicer or PrusaSlicer each part takes the colour of its filament. A 3MF with several objects, such as a project with one object per plate, comes in as one body per object; modifiers, negative volumes and support blockers from the slicer are left out. Colour painted onto faces in the slicer is not read. From Tinkercad: An STL or OBJ export from Tinkercad comes in as geometry like any other mesh, and an OBJ keeps the colours. The real shapes come across with a free tool from the community: Export to layerling by taylormadearmy, a bookmark that converts a Tinkercad design in your browser into a .lyl file, which you open here with 「layerlingデザインを開く」. It is not part of layerling and we have not tested it ourselves yet; its author tested it on Windows with Chrome. A design saved with a newer layerling may hold things your version does not know yet, such as a new shape, a new setting or fonts of one's own. If layerling cannot open it for that reason, the message names both versions. If it opens, the notice says that newer things may look different here. Either way, reloading the page helps: layerling.com always serves the newest version. The installed app picks it up the next time it starts; on your own server you install the update. Template pictures are added in sketch mode, see Sketches.

A scanned or sculpted mesh often has far more triangles than its shape needs, and every one of them is carried along while you move, cut and save. 「メッシュを簡略化」 in the Modify group (or in the right-click menu of the body) shows the mesh as it is next to what a chosen share of its triangles would leave of it; both views turn and zoom together with the mouse buttons of the workplane. Set how much to keep as a percentage or a number of triangles, and 「簡略化」 takes the lighter mesh. The result is a plain mesh: for the result of a cut or merge, 「グループを編集」 and its original parts are given up. With 「Keep edges and holes」 switched on, as it is to begin with, sharp edges and the rims of holes stay exactly where they are while flat faces still lose most of their triangles; switched off, the simplifier may round them off to reach a lower count. If the simplifier stops above the number you asked for, the window says so and why: with 「Keep edges and holes」 on, a body made of flat faces and sharp edges, such as boxes and wedges, often cannot lose more. Cutting, merging and intersecting an imported mesh is calculated in your browser, so the workspace settings limit how many triangles such a mesh may have (「読み込んだメッシュの切り抜き上限」). A mesh above the limit is not processed, and the message names its triangle count; simplify the mesh first, or raise the limit if your computer can take it.

An STL, OBJ or 3MF file holds only triangles, even when the part was drawn in CAD with flat faces and round bores. 「Make exact」 in the 「変形」 group (or in the right-click menu of the body) looks through those triangles for the planes, cylinders, cones, spheres and tori they were made of and rebuilds the body from them as an exact CAD body: a bore becomes one real cylinder with a round rim instead of a hundred narrow strips. After that, 「フィレット」 and 「面取り」 follow one clean edge, 「面を削除」 takes away a whole rounding or the wall of a hole, and a STEP export carries the real faces. The status line says what was found, such as "planes: 9, cylinders: 4". What fits none of these surfaces stays as small flat facets, and the message says how much of the surface that is. A body that is mostly free-form, such as a figure or a sculpted shape, stays a mesh, and so does a mesh with gaps or crossed walls, which cannot close into a solid. Up to 400,000 triangles are taken, and a large mesh can take a few minutes. A larger mesh goes below that with 「メッシュを簡略化」 and 「Keep edges and holes」 switched on; otherwise take the mesh as it came, it comes out cleanest. One undo step brings the mesh back. For a small mesh with round faces, up to 4,000 triangles, the edge tools do this by themselves: rounding an edge of such an STL rebuilds it the same way first.

If layerling does something unexpected, save a 「バグ報告」: the link sits in the footer at the bottom, next to the forum. It is a ZIP file, because GitHub and many forums refuse a bare .lyl: inside are your design as a .lyl and a short text file with the version, browser, screen size, the last messages and any errors. The start page opens the ZIP like a backup, or you unpack it and open the .lyl. Nothing personal is in it. Attach the file to your post in the forum or on GitHub, so the problem can be followed with exactly your design. If layerling stops with an error, a window with the error message shows instead of a blank page. From it you can save the state of the design last stored in the browser as a .lyl file, go back to the overview, or start a new design. The error message from the window and the saved file help when you report it.

When layerling runs on your own computer or web server, it can offer a shared folder in which all users keep designs. The start page then holds the designs in two tabs, 「サーバー」 for the shared folder and one for this browser, each with the number of designs in it; the one with more designs comes first and is open. You create folders there, move designs by dragging and search across the whole folder. A design that lives there saves itself back to it. A design from this browser goes onto the server by dragging its card onto the 「サーバー」 tab, or with 「サーバーに置く」 in the card's menu. While the 「サーバー」 tab is open, 「新しい3Dデザインを作成」 and 「バックアップを戻す」 put the design into the server folder you have open, and 「すべてバックアップ」 packs every design of the server, in its folders, and its custom shapes into one ZIP file. The start page shows a design by its file name, so renaming a design, on its card or at the top of the editor, renames the file on the server too. Deleting a design or a folder removes it for good, together with its working copy in this browser. Custom shapes kept on the server sit in its folder Custom shapes, see Shapes. Two things make that quicker: 「すべてサーバーに置く」 on the start page puts every design of this browser on the server in one go, and ticking 「新しいデザインはサーバーに」 makes every new design start in the server folder, so it is saved there from the first change on. With the tick, everything else that makes a design starts there too: opening or importing a file, 「バックアップを戻す」 (with the backup's folders), duplicating and taking a state from the history, each into the server folder you had open; 「新しいフォルダー」 on the start page then makes a folder on the server. A design made in the first moments waits until the server has answered. When new designs must always start on the server and this browser holds none of its own, the start page shows only the server's designs. The tick is kept in this browser. A design that cannot go - its name is taken on the server, say - stays in the browser, and the message says how many. The other export formats (STL, 3MF, OBJ, STEP, SVG, PNG and the drawing) can go into the same folder: in the export window, 「サーバーに保存」 writes the file next to your design, or into the folder you have open on the start page for a design that is not on the server. A program that shares the folder, such as a slicer in Docker, can open it from there. The file does not appear in the list of designs. If a file of that name is already there, the message says so, and pressing the button again replaces it. That is not simultaneous editing: whoever opens a file works on a copy of their own. If somebody else has changed the file in the meantime, layerling refuses to overwrite it. On layerling.com this function is not switched on. How to set it up on your own server is described in the README on GitHub.

All keys at a glance, taken straight from the program so the list is always right. The shortcuts work as long as the workplane has the focus. While you type in a field they keep out of the way. On the Mac, Cmd applies wherever Ctrl is listed here. In the editor, 「キーボードショートカット」 in the 「ヘルプ」 area opens the same list as a window. The printer button in the window (「印刷またはPDFで保存」) prints the list on its own, black on white, the whole list on one side of an A4 or Letter sheet in three columns, to keep at hand as a quick reference; the print dialog of the browser also offers to save it as a PDF. The box at the top of the window searches the list: it keeps only the shortcuts whose sentence, group or keys contain every word you type, so "fillet" or "ctrl+z" leaves just those rows. Capital letters and accents do not matter, and a single letter or digit finds that key and the words that start with it. The X at the end of the box empties it; with the box empty the whole list is back. The printer button prints what the window shows, so after a search it prints only the shortcuts found. The keyboard shortcuts window in the editor.

Can't find a tool? Press Ctrl+K or click the magnifying glass in the 「ヘルプ」 area, then type what you are looking for: a tool ("fillet", "mirror"), a shape ("cylinder") or a command ("export", "undo"). Move with the arrow keys and press Enter, or click the entry. The search understands the English and the German word alike and ignores capital letters and umlauts: "aushoehlen" finds 「中空にする」. Every entry shows the keys that do the same and the group of the ribbon it lives in, so you learn where it is. Entries that are greyed out cannot run right now, mostly because nothing is selected. They stay in the list so the search still tells you where the tool is. The guide you are reading has a search box too, at the top of every page: type a word or two and it lists the sections that contain all of them, with the matching words marked. Click one, or press Enter for the first, to jump straight there. The page it opens marks every place your words appear and scrolls to the first one in that section; Esc or a click on a mark clears them. A shape's name adds that shape to the workplane, just like clicking it in the shapes menu. With an empty field the search lists the commands you used last at the top. The name of a body in your design finds that body and selects it, which helps in a design with many parts. Bodies only appear once you type. A custom shape you saved is found by its name too, once you type, and a click puts it into the design as in the shapes panel. It works in sketch mode as well, with the sketch tools.

Any command of the command search can go on a key of your own: a tool you use all the time, a shape, 「作業平面の中央に置く」 or 「Open the shapes panel」. Open 「キーボードショートカット」 and click 「Add a key」 under 「Your own keys」 at the top of the window. Type a few letters of the command and click it, or press Enter for the first one. Press the key you want, alone or with Ctrl, Alt or Shift. Letters, digits and F1 to F12 can take a command. A key the editor already uses, one the browser keeps for itself (such as Ctrl+W) or one of your own keys is refused, and the window says what it does. Click a key in the list to change it, the X next to it to remove it, or 「Remove all my keys」 to start over. The key runs the command just as the command search does. If it cannot run right now, mostly because nothing is selected, the status bar says so. Your keys show next to their commands in the command search and on the printed list. They stay in this browser, like the theme. A key for a sketch tool works in sketch mode, a key for the 3D editor outside it. While you type in a field, your keys keep out of the way like all the others.

Cannot find where to read about a button or a field? Let the program take you there. Click the question mark in the 「ヘルプ」 area, or press Shift+F1. The pointer turns into a question mark, and whatever lies under it is outlined. Click a button, a field, a switch, a handle, a group of the ribbon or the title bar of a window. It does not do what it normally does. A small window opens instead, with the name of the element, a short summary of the part of this guide that is about it, up to two more places that mention it, and 「ガイドで開く」. The help is about the element you pointed at, not about the whole window around it. An element without a name of its own uses the nearest one around it; inside a window it falls back on that window's question mark. 「ガイドで開く」 opens the guide at that section in a new tab. There the section is outlined in colour, from its heading to its end, so you see where it starts and stops. If the guide says nothing about the element, the window says so and offers 「ガイドを検索」. Esc, or the question mark again, leaves the mode. On a touch screen there is no hover: a tap on an element opens the window straight away. The window moves by its title bar like the other windows. The program finds the section by the name of the element - the label on a button, the name of a field - because this guide writes every button as it is called in the program. It looks it up in the same search as the box at the top of each guide page, in the language you are using, and runs entirely in your browser.
